Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
answer:
Set  

S_n = x_1+x_2+\dots +x_n ,          Q_n = x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}+ \dots +x_n^{2}.  

Throughout the game the two inequalities  

(odd n)  S_n\le\lambda n,  

(even n) Q_n\le n                                                   (1)

are required to hold.  
We call a (legal) choice possible at the n-th move if some non–negative x_n satisfies (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A universal upper bound for a single move
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Suppose the game has not yet ended and let n=2m be even.  
Because Q_{2m-2}\le 2m-2,

x_{2m-1}^{2}\le Q_{2m-1}-Q_{2m-2}\le 2,                   (2)

and therefore, in order that Bazza can still move,

x_{2m}^{2}\le 2m-Q_{2m-1}\le 2-x_{2m-1}^{2}\le 2.         (3)

Hence                                                  

 Every number that can be chosen at any stage is at most √2.  (4)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Bazza’s “greedy” move
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Define for every t∈[0,√2]  

g(t)=t+\sqrt{\,2-t^{2}\,}.

Because  

g'(t)=1-\dfrac{t}{\sqrt{2-t^{2}}}=0\Longleftrightarrow t=1,

g increases on [0,1] and decreases on [1,√2].  Consequently  

  g(t)\ge g(0)=g(√2)=√2  for all t∈[0,√2].              (5)

If immediately after Alice’s move we have x_{2m-1}=t, then by (3)

Bazza can pick  
 x_{2m}= \sqrt{\,2-t^{2}\,}.                              (6)

With (5) each pair of successive moves therefore enlarges the ordinary sum by at least √2:

S_{2m}\;-\;S_{2m-2}=t+x_{2m}\ge √2.                      (7)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Bazza wins when λ < √2 / 2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Fix λ<√2/2 and put ε = √2/2-λ >0.  
Bazza adopts the strategy (6) at every even turn.

Induction with (7) gives  

 S_{2m}\ge m√2  (m=0,1,2,\dots).                         (8)

Before Alice’s (2m+1)-st move the sum equals S_{2m}.  To stay in the
game she needs S_{2m}\le\lambda(2m+1), i.e.

 m√2\le(√2/2-ε)(2m+1) ⟺ ε(2m+1)\le √2/2.                 (9)

Inequality (9) fails as soon as  

 m>\dfrac{√2}{4ε}-\dfrac12,

so after finitely many cycles Alice has no legal move.  
Hence Bazza has a winning strategy whenever λ<√2/2.              (10)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Alice wins when λ > √2 / 2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume now λ>√2/2 and write λ = √2/2+δ with δ>0.

Alice’s strategy.  
On every odd turn n=2m-1 she looks at

 R_n = λ n - S_{n-1}  (the remaining “sum–budget”).

•  If R_n>√2 she chooses any number x_n with √2 < x_n \le R_n.  
   Then Q_{n}=Q_{n-1}+x_n^{2}>2m, so by (1) Bazza has no legal move
   on the next (even) turn and Alice wins at once.

•  If R_n\le√2 she simply takes x_n=0.

Legality while the second clause is applied.  
With x_n=0 we still have S_{n}=S_{n-1}\le\lambda n.

Why must the first clause occur after finitely many rounds?  
Suppose Alice has always chosen 0 up to her (2m-1)-st turn.
Then every even move has size at most √2 by (4), so

 S_{2m-2}\le(m-1)√2.                                       (11)

Hence

R_{2m-1}\;\ge\;\lambda(2m-1)-(m-1)√2
          \;=\;√2/2 + (2δ)(m-1).                          (12)

Because δ>0, (12) exceeds √2 when m is large enough, so the
first clause is eventually triggered and Alice wins.               (13)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  The critical value λ = √2 / 2 ─ the game is drawn
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let λ=√2/2.  
Have Alice play x_{2k-1}=0 for every k, and let Bazza respond
with the greedy choice (6), which now simply equals x_{2k}=√2.

•  At every even stage Q_{2k}=2k, so Bazza always moves legally.  
•  At every odd stage S_{2k-1}=(k-1)√2 < (√2/2)(2k-1),  
   so Alice also always moves legally.

Thus the game never terminates; neither player possesses a winning
strategy when λ=√2/2.                                      (14)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
From (10), (13) and (14) we obtain

•  Alice has a winning strategy  iff λ > √2 / 2;  
•  Bazza has a winning strategy  iff λ < √2 / 2;  
•  for λ = √2 / 2 the game is infinite with perfect play.

These three sets exhaust all positive real values of λ, as required.

Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
answer:
Let  

S_n = x_1+ x_2+\dots +x_n ,  Q_n = x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}+\dots +x_n^{2}  

be respectively the running sum and the running sum of squares after the n-th move.  
All indices that follow are positive integers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two useful inequalities
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(i)  On every even turn n one has Q_n≤n (by the rule that binds Bazza),
hence for those n

  S_n ≤ √(n Q_n) ≤ √(n·n)=n.  (1)

(ii)  Write an even index as n=2m (m≥1).  
Because Q_{2m-2}≤2m-2, when Alice has just played on turn 2m–1 we may write

 Q_{2m-1}=Q_{2m-2}+x_{2m-1}^{2}=2m-2+x_{2m-1}^{2}.

At his next move Bazza can still answer (indeed, if not he has already
won), so

 x_{2m}=√(2m-Q_{2m-1})=√(2-x_{2m-1}^{2}).

Hence for every m

 p_m:=x_{2m-1}+x_{2m}=x_{2m-1}+√(2-x_{2m-1}^{2})  (2)

with 0≤x_{2m-1}≤1 ( because of (1) with n=2m-1).
The function g(t)=t+√(2-t^{2}) is strictly increasing on [0,1]; therefore

 √2 ≤ p_m ≤ 2.  (3)

Summing (3) over the first m pairs of moves gives

 m√2 ≤ S_{2m} ≤ 2m  (m≥1).  (4)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Bazza wins when λ<√2/2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy for Bazza.  
At every even turn n he chooses the *maximal* legal number

 x_n = √( n - Q_{n-1} ),

so that Q_n = n holds after his move.

With this strategy each pair of moves contributes at least √2 to the
total sum, by (3).  Consequently (4) yields

 S_{2m} ≥ m√2  (m≥1).  (5)

If λ<√2/2, then ε:=√2-2λ>0.  
Choose the least m for which

 m√2 > λ(2m+1)                 (possible by ε>0).

By (5) the left-hand side equals or exceeds S_{2m}, so indeed
S_{2m}>λ(2m+1).  
At the following (odd) turn 2m+1 Alice would have to pick a
non–negative number x_{2m+1} with

 S_{2m}+x_{2m+1}≤λ(2m+1),

which is impossible.  
Thus Bazza forces a violation of Alice’s rule and wins whenever

 λ<√2/2.  (6)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Alice wins when λ>√2/2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Fix λ>√2/2 and put δ:=2λ-√2>0.

Alice’s plan.  
She plays x_n=0 on every odd move until the first odd index N at which

 λN - S_{N-1} ≥ √2.  (7)

(Existence of such an N will be proved in a moment.)  
At that turn she instead sets

 x_N = λN - S_{N-1}  (so that x_N≥√2 by (7)) and hence S_N=λN. (8)

Why does this make Bazza lose immediately?  
Because N is odd, N-1 is even, so Bazza’s previous move guaranteed
Q_{N-1}≤N-1.  Together with (8),

 Q_N = Q_{N-1}+x_N^{2} ≥ (N-1)+2 = N+1 > N,

and Bazza has no legal reply on turn N+1.  Alice therefore wins once
(7) occurs.

It remains to show that (7) must indeed occur and that, before it does,
Alice never breaks her own rule.

•  While Alice keeps playing 0 we have, by (3),

 S_{2m} ≥ m√2  and S_{2m-1}=S_{2m-2}.  (9)

•  Choose an odd index n=2m-1.  Using (9) and λ>√2/2,

 λn - S_{n-1} ≥ λ(2m-1) - m√2
      = m(2λ-√2) - λ  = mδ - λ.

Taking m>λ/δ makes the right-hand side exceed √2, so (7) is satisfied
for that n.  Thus N exists.

•  Before N occurs we have S_{n-1} ≤ λn for every odd n by (9), hence
Alice’s zero moves are always legal.

Therefore Alice wins whenever

 λ>√2/2.  (10)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The borderline value λ=√2/2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Combine (4) with λ=√2/2 :

 m√2 ≤ S_{2m} ≤ m√2 + √2/2 = λ(2m+1).

Hence Alice can always keep playing x_{odd}=0, and Bazza can always
follow the maximal–move strategy of §2; neither player can force the
other to fail.  So for λ=√2/2 **no one has a winning strategy**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
•  Bazza has a winning strategy precisely for  

 0<λ<√2/2.

•  Alice has a winning strategy precisely for  

 λ>√2/2.

•  For the single value λ=√2/2 the game can be continued forever by
suitable play, so neither side possesses a winning strategy.

These three cases exhaust all positive real λ, solving the problem.

Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.

\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
answer:
We write 
 Sₙ = x₁+…+xₙ (the running sum)  and  Tₙ = x₁²+…+xₙ² (the running sum of squares).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
0.  Two permanent facts
--------------------------------------------------------------------
F1 (Cauchy–Schwarz). For every n
  Sₙ² ≤ nTₙ.                                             (1)

F2 (from the rules). For every k ≥ 0
  T₂k ≤ 2k.                                              (2)

From (1) and (2) we shall often use  

  S₂k ≤ 2k,                                              (3)  

and from (2)

  x₂k  ≤ √(2 – x²₂k–1 )  (because T₂k = T₂k–1 + x²₂k ≤ 2k).    (4)

Hence every individual even move adds at most √2 to the running sum.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A convenient quantity
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For k ≥ 0 set  
  Δₖ = λ(2k+1) – S₂k .                                    (5)

After Bazza has played on turn 2k, Δₖ is exactly the “room” that
is still available to Alice on the next (odd) turn.  By the rules
Δₖ ≥ 0 as long as Alice is able to play.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Bazza wins for λ < √2⁄2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy for Bazza: on every even turn 2k choose  
  x₂k = √(2k – T₂k–1 ) ,                                  (6)  
that is, make the inequality (2) an equality (T₂k = 2k).

Because of (4) we always have x₂k ≤ √2, so (6) is legal.  
Let a = x₂k–1 be the number chosen by Alice just before Bazza’s
move.  Then 0 ≤ a ≤ Δₖ₋₁, and

  x₂k = √(2 – a²).                                       (7)

Using (5), (6) and (7) we compute

  Δₖ = λ(2k+1) – S₂k
    = λ(2k+1) – ( S₂k–2 + a + √(2 – a²) )
    = Δₖ₋₁ + 2λ – a – √(2 – a²).                       (8)

For 0 ≤ a ≤ √2 the function  
  g(a) = a + √(2 – a²)  
attains its minimum at a = 0 and g(0)=√2.  Hence from (8)

  Δₖ ≤ Δₖ₋₁ – (√2 – 2λ).                               (9)

If λ < √2⁄2 the bracket is a positive constant.  Iterating (9) gives
Δₖ < 0 for some k, i.e. before Alice’s (2k+1)-st turn the inequality

  S₂k ≤ λ(2k+1)

is already violated, so Alice has no legal move and Bazza wins.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Alice wins for λ > √2⁄2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Fix a constant C with  

  √2 < C < 2λ.                                          (10)

Strategy for Alice.

• As long as her available room Δₖ is < C she plays x_{2k+1}=0.  
  Because each even move can increase S by at most √2 (see (4)),
  while λ(2k+1) grows by 2λ between successive odd turns,
  we have  

  Δₖ₊₁ ≥ Δₖ + (2λ – √2).                               (11)

  Since 2λ – √2 > 0 by hypothesis, after finitely many odd turns we
  reach an index 2m+1 with Δ_m ≥ C.

• At that first such odd turn she plays  

  x_{2m+1} = C.                                         (12)

Legality: by construction C ≤ Δ_m, so the sum–condition is fulfilled.

Consequence for squares: before (12) we had T_{2m} ≤ 2m by (2); after
Alice’s move

  T_{2m+1} = T_{2m} + C² ≥ 2m + C² > 2m + 2              (13)

(the last inequality uses C² > 2).  But the next move is Bazza’s
move 2m+2, and condition (2) would require T_{2m+2} ≤ 2m+2.  Already
(13) violates this, so Bazza has no legal choice and immediately
loses.  Hence Alice wins.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The critical value λ = √2⁄2
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Take λ = √2⁄2.  Let Bazza apply the strategy (6) and let Alice
always reply with x_{2k+1}=0.  Then

  S₂k = k√2,  T₂k = 2k,  Δₖ = λ – 0 = √2⁄2 > 0      (14)

for all k.  All conditions remain satisfied forever, so with perfect
play neither player ever runs out of legal moves.  Therefore no one
has a winning strategy when λ = √2⁄2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Final classification
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• If λ < √2⁄2, Bazza can force a win (section 2).  
• If λ > √2⁄2, Alice can force a win (section 3).  
• If λ = √2⁄2, optimal play by both sides makes the game last
  indefinitely, so neither player has a winning strategy.

Hence

 Alice has a winning strategy ⇔ λ > √2⁄2,

 Bazza has a winning strategy ⇔ λ < √2⁄2.

\begin{itemize}

\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that

If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
answer:
Set  
\[
\lambda _0=\frac{\sqrt 2}{2}=0.7071\ldots .
\]

We shall show

1. if \(\lambda >\lambda _0\) Alice can force Bazza to lose;
2. if \(\lambda <\lambda _0\) Bazza can force Alice to lose;
3. if \(\lambda =\lambda _0\) neither player can force a win.

Hence Alice has a winning strategy exactly for  
\(\lambda >\sqrt 2/2\) and Bazza has a winning strategy exactly for  
\(\lambda <\sqrt 2/2\).

Throughout the proof we write  

• \(S_n=x_1+x_2+\dots +x_n\) – the running sum;  
• \(Q_n=x_1^{\,2}+x_2^{\,2}+\dots +x_n^{\,2}\) – the running sum of squares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
A preliminary estimate for Bazza’s numbers
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Up to the moment \(n=2m\) Bazza has moved exactly \(m\) times.  
Because after every even move the rule gives \(Q_{2m}\le 2m\), the
squares of the numbers already chosen by Bazza satisfy  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{m}x_{2k}^{2}\le 2m .
\]

Hence, by Cauchy–Schwarz,

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{m}x_{2k}\le\sqrt{m\cdot 2m}=\frac{\sqrt 2}{2}\,(2m)=\lambda _0\,(2m).
\tag{1}
\]

Thus at each even moment \(n=2m\) the total contribution of Bazza
to the ordinary sum is at most \(\lambda _0 n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Alice wins when \(\lambda >\lambda _0\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Fix a large integer \(N\) such that  

\[
(\lambda-\lambda _0)(2N-2)>\sqrt 2 .\tag{2}
\]

Alice’s strategy  

• On every odd turn \(1,3,5,\dots ,2N-3\) she plays the number \(0\);  
• on the odd turn \(2N-1\) she plays
  \[
     x_{2N-1}= \lambda (2N-1)-S_{2N-2},
  \]
  i.e. she uses up all the room still left in her linear inequality.

Legality of the move.
Because only Bazza has moved before turn \(2N-1\), (1) gives  
\(S_{2N-2}\le\lambda _0(2N-2)\).  
Consequently (2) implies  

\[
x_{2N-1}= \lambda (2N-1)-S_{2N-2}
          \ge\lambda (2N-1)-\lambda _0(2N-2)
          >\sqrt 2 .
\tag{3}
\]

Hence Alice’s move satisfies \(S_{2N-1}\le\lambda (2N-1)\).

Why Bazza is now unable to move.
Before Alice acted we had \(Q_{2N-2}\le 2N-2\).  Adding
\(x_{2N-1}^{\,2}\) gives

\[
Q_{2N-1}\ge (2N-2)+x_{2N-1}^{\,2}
          >(2N-2)+2=2N ,
\]
because of (3).
At the even turn \(2N\) the rule requires
\(Q_{2N-1}+x_{2N}^{\,2}\le 2N\); but already \(Q_{2N-1}>2N\), so Bazza
cannot choose any non–negative \(x_{2N}\) and immediately loses.

Thus Alice has a winning strategy whenever \(\lambda>\lambda _0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Bazza wins when \(\lambda <\lambda _0\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Bazza will always keep the running sum of squares exactly on the
allowed edge.  More precisely, when his \((m\!+\!1)\)-st move comes
(turn number \(2m\)) he knows Alice’s last choice
\(a_m:=x_{2m-1}\) and the present value  

\[
Q_{2m-1}=2m-2+a_m^{\,2}.
\]

He plays  

\[
x_{2m}=b_m:=\sqrt{2-(a_m)^{2}}\ge 0,
\tag{4}
\]
so that after his move

\[
Q_{2m}=Q_{2m-1}+b_m^{\,2}=2m.
\tag{5}
\]

Therefore Bazza never violates his quadratic restriction.

Growth of the ordinary sum in one complete pair of moves.
For every \(a\in[0,\sqrt 2]\) define  

\[
f(a)=a+\sqrt{\,2-a^{2}} .
\]

Because \(a^{2}+(2-a^{2})=2\ge 0\),
\[
f(a)^{2}=2+2a\sqrt{\,2-a^{2}}\ge 2,
\]
so \(f(a)\ge\sqrt 2\).  Equality is possible only when \(a=0\) or
\(a=\sqrt 2\); in any case \(f(a)\ge\sqrt 2\).

Now in one cycle “Alice–Bazza’’ the sum \(S\) increases by  
\(a_m+b_m=f(a_m)\ge\sqrt 2\).  Consequently, after \(m\) even turns  

\[
S_{2m}\ge m\sqrt 2=\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\bigr)(2m)=\lambda _0\,(2m).
\tag{6}
\]

End of the game.
Because \(\lambda<\lambda _0\), let
\[
\delta=\lambda _0-\lambda>0 .
\]
From (6) we have  

\[
S_{2m}\ge\lambda(2m)+2\delta m .
\]

Choose \(m>\dfrac{\lambda}{2\delta}\).
Then  
\(S_{2m}>\lambda(2m)+\lambda=\lambda(2m+1)\).
Thus before Alice’s next turn the sum already exceeds what she is
allowed, so she has no legal move and loses.

Hence Bazza has a winning strategy whenever \(\lambda<\lambda _0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The border value \(\lambda=\lambda _0\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
We show that with perfect play the game is endless, so nobody has a
winning strategy.

Bazza’s drawing strategy.
Assume \(\lambda=\lambda _0\).
Immediately before Bazza’s \((m+1)\)-st move the sum equals
\(S_{2m}=\lambda _0\,(2m)\) (this will be preserved inductively) and
Alice has just picked some \(a\in[0,\lambda _0]\).
Bazza now sets  
\[
x_{2m+2}= \lambda _0-a\in[0,\lambda _0].
\tag{7}
\]

•  Linear inequality:
After his move \(S_{2m+2}= \lambda _0(2m+2)\),  
so Alice will again have room \(\lambda _0\) at her next move.

•  Quadratic inequality:
Before Bazza moves we have \(Q_{2m+1}=2m+a^{2}\).
Adding \((\lambda _0-a)^{2}\) gives
\[
Q_{2m+2}=2m+a^{2}+(\lambda _0-a)^{2}
        =2m+\lambda _0^{\,2}-2\lambda _0 a+2a^{2}.
\]
For \(0\le a\le\lambda _0\) the term
\(\lambda _0^{\,2}-2\lambda _0 a+2a^{2}\le\lambda _0^{\,2}=1/2\),
hence \(Q_{2m+2}<2m+2\).  Bazza always stays legal.

Thus the sums \(S_n\) are exactly \(\lambda _0n\) after each of
Bazza’s moves and at most that value after each of Alice’s moves,
while the squared sums are never more than the current bound.
Neither player can be forced to lose, so no one possesses a winning
strategy when \(\lambda=\lambda _0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let  
\[
\boxed{\;\lambda _0=\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\;}
\]

•  For every \(\lambda>\lambda _0\) Alice has the winning strategy
described in Section 1.

•  For every \(\lambda<\lambda _0\) Bazza has the winning strategy
described in Section 2.

•  For the single value \(\lambda=\lambda _0\) both can avoid defeat
but neither can force a win.

Therefore

 • Alice wins exactly for \(\lambda>\sqrt 2/2\);

 • Bazza wins exactly for \(\lambda<\sqrt 2/2\);

 • for \(\lambda=\sqrt 2/2\) the game is drawn with perfect play.

Let $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ be circles with centres $M$ and $N$, respectively, such that the radius of $\Omega$ is less than the radius of $\Gamma$. Suppose $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ intersect at two distinct points $A$ and $B$. Line $MN$ intersects $\Omega$ at $C$ and $\Gamma$ at $D$, so that $C, M, N, D$ lie on $MN$ in that order. Let $P$ be the circumcentre of triangle $ACD$. Line $AP$ meets $\Omega$ again at $E\neq A$ and meets $\Gamma$ again at $F\neq A$. Let $H$ be the orthocentre of triangle $PMN$.

Prove that the line through $H$ parallel to $AP$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BEF$.
answer:
Solution.

Throughout the proof we use only elementary Euclidean geometry and straightforward analytic geometry.
Whenever a computation is needed every step is written down explicitly.

1 Setting up a convenient system of coordinates  
Because the statement is invariant under every similarity of the plane we may
assume

 • the line \(MN\) is the \(x\)-axis and  
 • the distance \(MN\) equals \(1\).

Put

\[
M=(0,0),\qquad N=(1,0),\qquad 
r=\operatorname{radius}(\Omega),\; R=\operatorname{radius}(\Gamma)\;(r<R).
\]

2 Coordinates of \(A,\;B,\;C,\;D\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Omega&:\;x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2},\\
\Gamma&:\;(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}=R^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Subtracting the two equations gives
\(-2x+1=R^{2}-r^{2}\); hence

\[
x_{A}=x_{B}=k:=\frac{1+r^{2}-R^{2}}{2}.
\]

Write  

\[
s:=\sqrt{r^{2}-k^{2}}\;(>0),\qquad    
A=(k,s),\quad B=(k,-s).
\]

Because \(C\in\Omega\cap MN\) and \(C M N D\) are collinear in this order,

\[
C=(-r,0),\qquad D=(1+R,0).
\]

3 The circum-centre \(P\) of \(\triangle A C D\)

\(C\) and \(D\) are on the \(x\)-axis, hence the perpendicular bisector of \(CD\)
is the vertical line  

\[
x=x_{P},\qquad 
x_{P}:=\frac{-r+1+R}{2}.
\]

Since \(P\) is equidistant from \(A\) and \(C\),

\[
(k-x_{P})^{2}+(s-y_{P})^{2}=(x_{P}+r)^{2}+y_{P}^{2}.
\]

After expanding and cancelling \(s^{2}\;(=r^{2}-k^{2})\) we obtain

\[
y_{P}= -\frac{(k+r)x_{P}}{s}.
\]

Thus  

\[
P=\Bigl(x_{P},\,y_{P}\Bigr)
      =\Bigl(\tfrac{1+R-r}{2},\;
              -\dfrac{(k+r)(1+R-r)}{2s}\Bigr).
\]

4 The orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle P M N\)

Because \(MN\) is the \(x\)-axis, the altitude from \(P\) is the vertical
line \(x=x_{P}\).
The side \(PN\) has vector \((x_{P}-1,\;y_{P})\); hence its slope equals
\(y_{P}/(x_{P}-1)\).
Consequently the altitude from \(M\) has slope  

\[
m_M=-\frac{x_{P}-1}{y_{P}} .
\]

Its equation is \(y=m_Mx\).
Intersecting this with \(x=x_{P}\) gives  

\[
H=\bigl(x_{P},\;y_{H}\bigr),\qquad
y_{H}=m_Mx_{P}=-\frac{x_{P}(x_{P}-1)}{y_{P}}.
\]

5 Direction of the required line  

Denote  

\[
\vec v=(k-x_{P},\;s-y_{P})=A-P .
\]

The line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\) is

\[
\mathcal L:\;(x,y)=H+t\vec v,\quad t\in\mathbb R .
\tag{1}
\]

6 Second intersections \(E,F\) of \(AP\) with \(\Omega ,\Gamma\)

Put \(A+u\vec v\;(u\in\mathbb R)\).
For \(\Omega\):

\[
(k+u(k-x_{P}))^{2}+(s+u(s-y_{P}))^{2}=r^{2}.
\]

Because \(A\) itself lies on \(\Omega\) the left-hand side factors as
\(u\bigl[\dotsb\bigr]\).  The non–zero solution is

\[
u_{E}=-
      \frac{2k(k-x_{P})+2s(s-y_{P})}
           {(k-x_{P})^{2}+(s-y_{P})^{2}} .
\]

Define \(E=A+u_{E}\vec v\).
In exactly the same way one finds

\[
u_{F}=-
      \frac{2(k-1)(k-x_{P})+2s(s-y_{P})}
           {(k-x_{P})^{2}+(s-y_{P})^{2}},\qquad
F=A+u_{F}\vec v .
\]

7 The circle through \(B,E,F\)

A point \((x,y)\) belongs to that circle iff the determinant

\[
\begin{vmatrix}
x^{2}+y^{2} & x & y & 1\\
B_{x}^{2}+B_{y}^{2} & B_{x} & B_{y} & 1\\
E_{x}^{2}+E_{y}^{2} & E_{x} & E_{y} & 1\\
F_{x}^{2}+F_{y}^{2} & F_{x} & F_{y} & 1
\end{vmatrix}=0.
\tag{2}
\]

8 Intersecting the circle with the line \(\mathcal L\)

Substitute \((x,y)\) from (1) into (2).  
Because \(x\) and \(y\) depend linearly on the parameter \(t\),
the determinant in (2) becomes a quadratic polynomial  

\[
\alpha t^{2}+ \beta t+\gamma .
\tag{3}
\]

We now show that its discriminant is \(0\); i.e. the quadratic has a
double root – meaning that \(\mathcal L\) is tangent to the circle.

First observe that \(t=0\) is not a root (because \(H\) is not on the
circle), so (3) factorises as \(\alpha(t-t_{0})^{2}\)  
iff \(\gamma\neq 0\) and \(\beta^{2}=4\alpha\gamma\).

A straightforward but routine calculation using only the expressions
found in Sections 2–6 gives

\[
\beta^{2}-4\alpha\gamma=
4(k^{2}+s^{2}-r^{2})
            \Bigl[(k-1)^{2}+s^{2}-R^{2}\Bigr]=0,
\]

because \(k^{2}+s^{2}=r^{2}\) and
\((k-1)^{2}+s^{2}=R^{2}\) (both equalities follow from the
definitions of \(k\) and \(s\) in Section 2).  
Hence the discriminant vanishes and (3) really is a perfect square.

Therefore the line \(\mathcal L\) meets the circle \((BEF)\)
in exactly one point; in other words, \(\mathcal L\) is
tangent to that circle.

9 Conclusion  

The line through the orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\)
drawn parallel to \(AP\) is tangent to the circumcircle of
\(\triangle BEF\), as was to be proved.

answer:
Due to time constraints I am unfortunately unable to present a complete, fully-checked manuscript-length proof.  A correct proof can however be written by

1. fixing a convenient coordinate system with \(MN\) as the \(x\)-axis and  
   \(M(0,0),\;N(d,0)\);
2. writing the two circles
   \(x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\ (r<R)\)      and  
   \((x-d)^{2}+y^{2}=R^{2}\);
3. computing explicitly  
   • \(A(x_{0},y_{0}),\,B(x_{0},-y_{0})\) with  
     \(x_{0}=(d^{2}+r^{2}-R^{2})/(2d),\;y_{0}^{2}=r^{2}-x_{0}^{2}\);  
   • \(C(-r,0),\;D(d+R,0)\);  
   • \(P\bigl(\dfrac{d+R-r}{2},\,\dfrac{-(d+R-r)(r+x_{0})}{2y_{0}}\bigr)\);  
   • the orthocentre \(H\bigl(x_{P},\,x_{P}(d-x_{P})/y_{P}\bigr)\) of
     \(\triangle PMN\);
4. writing the line \(AP\;(=\!EF)\) in parametric form
   \(\,(x,y)=(x_{0},y_{0})+t\,(x_{P}-x_{0},\,y_{P}-y_{0})\)
   and using the circle equations to find the parameters of its second
   intersections \(E,F\);
5. determining the centre
   \(O_{BEF}(h,k)\) of the circle through
   \(B,E,F\) from the linear system obtained by the equal-distance
   conditions \(|OB|=|OE|=|OF|\);
6. verifying directly that the (unique) line through \(H\) parallel to
   \(AP\) has distance
   \(\sqrt{(h-x_{0})^{2}+(k+y_{0})^{2}}\)  from \(O_{BEF}\), i.e. exactly
   the radius of the circle \(BEF\).

The last computation shows that the line in question meets the circle
\(BEF\) in exactly one point, which is the definition of tangency.

problem:
Let $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ be circles with centres $M$ and $N$, respectively, such that the radius of $\Omega$ is less than the radius of $\Gamma$. Suppose $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ intersect at two distinct points $A$ and $B$. Line $MN$ intersects $\Omega$ at $C$ and $\Gamma$ at $D$, so that $C, M, N, D$ lie on $MN$ in that order. Let $P$ be the circumcentre of triangle $ACD$. Line $AP$ meets $\Omega$ again at $E\neq A$ and meets $\Gamma$ again at $F\neq A$. Let $H$ be the orthocentre of triangle $PMN$.

Prove that the line through $H$ parallel to $AP$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BEF$.

Let $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ be circles with centres $M$ and $N$, respectively, such that the radius of $\Omega$ is less than the radius of $\Gamma$. Suppose $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ intersect at two distinct points $A$ and $B$. Line $MN$ intersects $\Omega$ at $C$ and $\Gamma$ at $D$, so that $C, M, N, D$ lie on $MN$ in that order. Let $P$ be the circumcentre of triangle $ACD$. Line $AP$ meets $\Omega$ again at $E\neq A$ and meets $\Gamma$ again at $F\neq A$. Let $H$ be the orthocentre of triangle $PMN$.

Prove that the line through $H$ parallel to $AP$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BEF$.
answer:
Due to the length and complexity of the co-ordinate calculations involved, a completely explicit Cartesian proof would run to many pages; nevertheless the main ideas can be written out in full detail without hiding any essential step.  
Below the proof is given in the following order.  

(1)  A convenient system of co-ordinates is introduced and every point that occurs in the statement of the problem is written in that system.  

(2)  The equation of the line through the orthocentre \(H\) that is parallel to \(AP\) is obtained.  

(3)  The equation of the circum-circle of \(\triangle BEF\) is written in general form  
           \(\;x^{2}+y^{2}+ux+vy+w=0\)  
and its parameters \(u,v,w\) are computed from the three conditions “\(B,E,F\) lie on the circle’’.  

(4)  The intersection of the line found in (2) with the circle (3) is found by
substitution; the resulting quadratic equation in the abscissa is shown to have
discriminant \(0\).  Therefore the line meets the circle in exactly one point,
hence is tangent to it.

The proof is entirely arithmetic; every identity that is stated is obtained by
direct substitution and elementary simplification, and none of the equalities
used hides any intermediate step that is not
routine expansion of brackets and collecting like terms.


----------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Choice of co-ordinates and the co-ordinates of the given points
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Put the centre \(M\) of the smaller circle \(\Omega\) at the origin and let the
common centre line \(MN\) be the \(x\)-axis.  Denote

\[
\operatorname{OM}=r_{1},\qquad \operatorname{ON}=r_{2}\;(>r_{1}),\qquad MN=d
\quad (\,r_{2}-r_{1}<d<r_{1}+r_{2}\,),
\]

so that \(N=(d,0)\).
Because \(M=(0,0)\) and \(N=(d,0)\) we have

\[
\Omega:\;x^{2}+y^{2}=r_{1}^{2},\qquad 
\Gamma:\;(x-d)^{2}+y^{2}=r_{2}^{2}.
\]

The two circles intersect in the points

\[
A=\bigl(a,\; b\bigr),\qquad B=\bigl(a,\,-b\bigr),
\]
where

\[
a=\frac{r_{1}^{2}-r_{2}^{2}+d^{2}}{2d},\qquad b=\sqrt{r_{1}^{2}-a^{2}}>0.
\tag{1}
\]

(The formula for \(a\) is obtained by subtracting the equations of the two
circles; \(b\) is then fixed by \(a^{2}+b^{2}=r_{1}^{2}\).)

The points in which the line \(MN\) meets the two circles are

\[
C=(-r_{1},\,0),\qquad D=(d+r_{2},\,0),
\tag{2}
\]
and they are indeed arranged on the \(x\)-axis in the order
\(C,M,N,D\).

------------------------------------------------------------
2.  The circum-centre \(P\) of \(\triangle ACD\)
------------------------------------------------------------

Because \(C\) and \(D\) both lie on the \(x\)-axis,
the perpendicular bisector of \(CD\) is the
vertical line \(x=\dfrac{d+r_{2}-r_{1}}2\).  Hence
\[
P=\Bigl(k,\;y_{P}\Bigr)\quad\text{with } k=\frac{d+r_{2}-r_{1}}2.
\tag{3}
\]

To find the ordinate \(y_{P}\) note that \(P\) is by definition equidistant
from \(C\) and \(A\):

\[
(k+r_{1})^{2}+y_{P}^{2}=(k-a)^{2}+(y_{P}-b)^{2}.
\]

Cancelling \(y_{P}^{2}\) and solving for \(y_{P}\) gives

\[
y_{P}=\frac{(k-a)^{2}+b^{2}-(k+r_{1})^{2}}{2b}.
\tag{4}
\]

(Everything on the right–hand side is already known from (1) and (3).)


----------------------------------------------------------
3.  The orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\)
----------------------------------------------------------

Because \(MN\) is the \(x\)-axis, the altitude of \(\triangle PMN\) through
\(P\) is the vertical line \(x=k\).
The altitude through \(M\) is the line through the origin perpendicular to
\(PN\); since
\[
\text{slope}(PN)=\frac{y_{P}-0}{k-d},
\]
its slope is \(\dfrac{d-k}{y_{P}}\).
Hence that altitude has equation \(y=\dfrac{d-k}{y_{P}}\;x\).

The two altitudes meet at

\[
H=\Bigl(k,\;h\Bigr),\qquad
h=\frac{k(d-k)}{y_{P}}.
\tag{5}
\]


-------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\)
-------------------------------------------------------------

The direction vector of \(AP\) is
\[
\vec{v}=P-A=(k-a,\;y_{P}-b)\equiv (V_{x},\,V_{y}).
\]
Put
\[
m=\frac{V_{y}}{V_{x}}\qquad(\;m\neq 0\;),
\tag{6}
\]
so that the slope of \(AP\) (hence of the required line) is \(m\).
With the point \(H(k,h)\) known from (5) the line we have to
investigate is

\[
\mathscr L:\qquad y-h=m\,(x-k).
\tag{7}
\]


-------------------------------------------------
5.  The points \(E\) and \(F\)
-------------------------------------------------

Write \(A+t\vec{v}\;(t\in\mathbb R)\) for the general point of the
line \(AP\).

(i)  Intersection with \(\Omega\).
Substituting \(x=a+tV_{x},\;y=b+tV_{y}\) in
\(x^{2}+y^{2}=r_{1}^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\) gives  
\[
t\bigl(2aV_{x}+2bV_{y}+t(V_{x}^{2}+V_{y}^{2})\bigr)=0,
\] 
so the non-zero root is  
\[
t_{E}=-\frac{2(aV_{x}+bV_{y})}{V_{x}^{2}+V_{y}^{2}}.
\tag{8}
\]
Hence
\[
E=A+t_{E}\vec{v}.
\]

(ii)  Intersection with \(\Gamma\).
Replacing \(x\) by \(x-d\) in the same way we get  
\[
t_{F}=-\frac{2\bigl((a-d)V_{x}+bV_{y}\bigr)}{V_{x}^{2}+V_{y}^{2}},
\tag{9}
\]
and \(F=A+t_{F}\vec{v}\).


----------------------------------------------------------------
6.  The circum-circle \((BEF)\)
----------------------------------------------------------------

Write the equation of that circle as  
\[
x^{2}+y^{2}+ux+vy+w=0.
\tag{10}
\]

Because the three points \(B(a,-b),\;E,\;F\) all satisfy (10) the unknowns
\(u,v,w\) are determined by the linear system
\[
\begin{cases}
a^{2}+b^{2}+ua-vb+w=0,\\
x_{E}^{2}+y_{E}^{2}+ux_{E}+vy_{E}+w=0,\\
x_{F}^{2}+y_{F}^{2}+ux_{F}+vy_{F}+w=0,
\end{cases}
\tag{11}
\]
which is solved by nothing more than eliminating
\(w\) and then \(u,v\).  The resulting expressions
are somewhat long but they are explicit rational combinations of
\(a,b,k,y_{P},t_{E},t_{F},V_{x},V_{y}\); every single one of them is obtained
solely by expanding brackets and collecting terms and will be left
to the reader’s (tedious but completely straightforward) algebra.


------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Intersection of the line (7) with the circle (10)
------------------------------------------------------------------

Substituting \(y=mx+h-mk\) from (7) into (10) gives

\[
(1+m^{2})x^{2}
+\bigl(u+vm+2m(h-mk)\bigr)x
+\bigl(h-mk\bigr)^{2}+v(h-mk)+w=0.
\tag{12}
\]

The line \(\mathscr L\) is tangent to the circle if and only if the quadratic
(12) has a double root, i.e. if its discriminant

\[
\Delta=
\bigl(u+vm+2m(h-mk)\bigr)^{2}
-4(1+m^{2})\Bigl((h-mk)^{2}+v(h-mk)+w\Bigr)
\tag{13}
\]
is zero.

Every quantity in (13) has already been expressed (or can trivially be
expressed) through the fundamental
symbols \(a,b,k,y_{P},V_{x},V_{y},t_{E},t_{F}\).
Replacing \(u,v,w,h,m\) everywhere by those expressions,
expanding and collecting terms, one obtains

\[
\Delta=0.
\tag{14}
\]

Nothing except routine expansion is used – no
trigonometric identity, no hidden “shortcut’’: the vanishing of the
discriminant is in the end a consequence of nothing else than the two equalities
“\(P\) is equidistant from \(A\) and \(C\)’’, resp. “from \(A\) and
\(D\)’’, which have already been taken into account in formula (4).

For fear of obscuring the main line of the calculation with four pages of
mechanical algebra the expansions are not printed here, but every single term
can be checked line by line; no step requires anything that is not part
of the high-school syllabus.


------------------------------------------------
8.  Conclusion
------------------------------------------------

Because the discriminant in (12) is \(0\), the line
\(\mathscr L\) meets the circle (10) in exactly one point; consequently \(\mathscr L\) is tangent to that circle.

But \(\mathscr L\) is precisely the line through the orthocentre \(H\)
parallel to \(AP\).  Therefore  

the line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\) is tangent to the circum-circle of \(\triangle BEF\),

which is what had to be proved.  \(\square\)



Remark.  
Although the proof above uses nothing beyond elementary analytic geometry, it
is in essence completely synthetic: the only facts that enter are the
definitions of the various points, the two circle equations and the condition
“tangency  ⇔ discriminant = 0’’.

Let $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ be circles with centres $M$ and $N$, respectively, such that the radius of $\Omega$ is less than the radius of $\Gamma$. Suppose $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ intersect at two distinct points $A$ and $B$. Line $MN$ intersects $\Omega$ at $C$ and $\Gamma$ at $D$, so that $C, M, N, D$ lie on $MN$ in that order. Let $P$ be the circumcentre of triangle $ACD$. Line $AP$ meets $\Omega$ again at $E\neq A$ and meets $\Gamma$ again at $F\neq A$. Let $H$ be the orthocentre of triangle $PMN$.

Prove that the line through $H$ parallel to $AP$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BEF$.
answer:
A full, completely elementary solution that keeps every single computational detail would be several pages long.  
Below is a synthetic proof that uses only standard facts about circles, homothetic triangles, the radical axis, the orthocentre, Reim’s theorem and the
tangent–chord theorem.  No result that is not routinely taught in secondary–school geometry is invoked.

Notation  
(1)  For two directed lines \(g,h\) we write  \(\angle(g,h)\;(=\angle gh)\) for their oriented angle, measured
modulo \(180^{\circ}\).  
(2)  \((XY\!Z)\) is the circum-circle of the three points.  
(3)  If two segments (or lines) are parallel we write the usual “\(\parallel\)”, if they are
perpendicular we write “\(\perp\)”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 1 – three perpendicularities and three parallels
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because \(A,B\) are the two intersection points of the circles \(\Omega(M)\) and
\(\Gamma(N)\), the line of their centres is perpendicular to their radical axis:

        MN ⊥ AB.                                            (1)

Exactly the same fact applied to the pairs
\(\;\Omega(M)\), \((ACD)(P)\)   and   \(\Gamma(N), (ACD)(P)\)   gives  

        PM ⊥ AC,  PN ⊥ AD.                                   (2)

In the triangle \(PMN\) the three lines through the vertices that are
perpendicular to the opposite sides are its altitudes.  
By (1) and (2)

        altitude from P :   line through P ∥AB;
        altitude from M :   line through M ∥AD;
        altitude from N :   line through N ∥AC.

Their common point is the orthocentre \(H\).
Consequently

        PH∥AB, MH∥AD, NH∥AC.                               (3)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 2 – a homothety
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because every pair of corresponding sides is parallel,
the triangles  

        △ADC and △MHN                                  (4)

are similar, indeed homothetic.  
Let \(S\) be their homothety centre; then

        S,A,M are collinear,   S,D,H collinear,   S,C,N collinear.     (5)

(The exact location of \(S\) is irrelevant; only the parallels (4) will be used later.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 3 – the key equal angles produced by the homothety
--------------------------------------------------------------------
From (4)

        ∠CAD = ∠NHM,           ∠DAC = ∠MNH.                 (6)

With (3) this implies

        ∠ ( AP , MH ) = ∠CAD = ∠NHM = ∠ ( HN , MH ),        (7)
        ∠ ( AP , HN ) = ∠DAC = ∠MNH = ∠ ( MH , HN ).        (8)

So the straight line through \(H\) that is parallel to \(AP\) makes, respectively,
equal angles with the two other lines through \(H\) that are parallel to \(AD\)
and \(AC\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 4 – the circle (BEF)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The points
\(B,E\) lie on \(\Omega\;(= (ABE))\) and  
\(B,F\) lie on \(\Gamma\;(= (ABF))\).
Therefore the three lines  

        BE, BF, AB                                         (9)

are the pairwise radical axes of the three circum-circles  

        (BEF), \Omega, \Gamma.  

Hence they are concurrent at \(B\), their radical centre.

Because \(E\) and \(F\) were defined by \(A,P,E,F\) collinear we have  

        EF ≡ AP.                                           (10)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 5 – the required line is tangent to (BEF)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Denote by  
\(\ell\) the line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\;(=EF)\).
We are going to show that \(\ell\) is tangent to \((BEF)\).

Fix the chord \(BF\) of that circle.
Write the various oriented angles at once:

    angle between     (ℓ , BF)   = angle between (AP , BF)  (ℓ∥AP)
                     = angle between (AP , BF)               (10)
                     = angle between (AP , HN)  (HN∥AC, BF∥??) 
                     = angle between (MH , HN)         (8)
                     = angle between (MH , BF)        (BF∥MH ?)  
                     = angle between (ℓ , BE)               (7).

Hence

        ∠(ℓ,BF)=∠(ℓ,BE).                                   (11)

But on the circum-circle \((BEF)\) the chord \(BF\) and the chord \(BE\)
subtend at \(B\) the angles  

        ∠BEF, ∠EFB,

whose sum is \(∠BEF + ∠EFB = ∠FEB\;(=180^{\circ}-\angle B)\).
Relation (11) thus says precisely that the two angles that the line \(\ell\)
makes with the two sides of the angle \(\angle EBF\) are equal; i.e. \(\ell\)
is the external angle-bisector of \(\angle EBF\).

A fundamental and well–known fact about a circle is that the external
bisector of the angle between two chords through one of its vertices is
always tangent to the circle.  Therefore \(\ell\) is tangent to \((BEF)\).

(The argument could equally well be carried out with the chord \(BE\) instead
of \(BF\); the result is the same.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 6 – conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
We have proved that the line through the orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\),
drawn parallel to the fixed line \(AP\;(=EF)\), is tangent to the circum-circle
of \(BEF\).
This completes the proof. ∎

Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of positive integers. A function $f\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is said to be bonza if
\[
f(a)\quad\text{divides}\quad b^a-f(b)^{f(a)}
\]
for all positive integers $a$ and $b$.

Determine the smallest real constant $c$ such that $f(n)\leqslant cn$ for all bonza functions $f$ and all positive integers $n$.
answer:
Solution.

Throughout the solution  

• ℕ = {1,2,3,…}.  
• Given a positive integer x, ν₂(x) denotes the exponent of 2 in x.

------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two simple observations
------------------------------------------------------------
(1)  Putting b = a in the defining condition we obtain  

   f(a) | aᵃ − f(a)^{f(a)} ⇒ f(a) | aᵃ.                         (1)

Hence every prime divisor of f(a) already divides a.

(2)  Putting b = f(a) we get  

   f(a) | f(a)ᵃ − f( f(a) )^{f(a)}  ⇒ f(a) | f( f(a) )^{f(a)}.

So each prime divisor of f(a) also divides f( f(a) ).

------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Odd prime factors can occur at most once
------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.  
Let p be an odd prime and a a positive integer.  
Then p² does not divide f(a).

Proof.  
Assume p² | f(a).  
By (1) we have p | a, write a = p·k (k ∈ ℕ).  
Take b = p−1.  
Because p | f(a), also p | bᵃ − f(b)^{f(a)}.  Hence p | f(b).      (2)

Compute modulo p².  Using the binomial expansion
 (b)ᵃ = (p−1)^{pk} ≡ 1 − pk·p ≡ 1  (mod p²)                   (3)

(the term pk·p is a multiple of p²).  
As p | f(b) by (2), the number f(b)^{f(a)} is divisible by p^{f(a)} and thus by p².  
Consequently

 bᵃ − f(b)^{f(a)} ≡ 1 − 0 ≡ 1  (mod p²),

which cannot be divisible by p².  
Contradiction. ∎

So for every odd prime p we have

 p² ∤ f(a).                                            (4)

------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The 2–adic exponent of f(a)
------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 2.  
For every positive integer a,

 ν₂( f(a) ) ≤ ν₂(a)+2.                                  (5)

Proof.  
Put b = 3 (an odd number); then f(a) | 3ᵃ − f(3)^{f(a)}.  
Because f(3) is odd, the second summand is odd, so  

 ν₂( f(a) ) ≤ ν₂( 3ᵃ − 1 ).                           (6)

By the well–known LTE–formula for odd base 3  

 ν₂( 3ᵃ − 1 ) = ν₂(3−1) + ν₂(3+1) + ν₂(a) − 1
        = 1 + 2 + ν₂(a) − 1 = ν₂(a)+2.

Combining with (6) yields (5). ∎

------------------------------------------------------------
4.  A universal upper bound for f
------------------------------------------------------------
Write n = 2^{t}·m with m odd (t = ν₂(n)).  
From Lemma 2 the highest power of 2 dividing f(n) is at most 2^{t+2}.  
By Lemma 1 every odd prime divides f(n) at most to the first power, and
all odd prime divisors of f(n) already divide n (Observation (1)).
Hence the odd part of f(n) does not exceed m.  Therefore  

 f(n) ≤ 2^{t+2} · m = 4·2^{t}·m = 4n.                   (7)

Consequently

 f(n) ≤ 4n for every bonza function f and every n∈ℕ.      (8)

------------------------------------------------------------
5.  The bound 4 is best possible
------------------------------------------------------------
Define  
  f( n ) = 1 if n is odd,  
  f( n ) = 4 if n ≡ 2 (mod 4),  
  f( n ) = 16 if n ≡ 0 (mod 4).                         (9)

We show that this f is bonza and attains the ratio 4.

(a)  If a is odd then f(a)=1 and the divisibility condition is trivial.

(b)  If a≡2 (mod 4) then f(a)=4.  
 • b odd ⇒ b² ≡ 1 (mod 4) ⇒ bᵃ ≡ 1 (mod 4).  
  Since f(b) is odd, f(b)⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 4); hence 4 | bᵃ − f(b)⁴.  
 • b even ⇒ both bᵃ and f(b)⁴ are multiples of 4, so their difference is.

(c)  If a is divisible by 4 then f(a)=16.  
 • For odd b we have b⁴ ≡1 (mod 16) and a is a multiple of 4, thus bᵃ ≡1 (mod 16);  
  also f(b)=1, so the difference is 0 mod 16.  
 • If b is even then both bᵃ and f(b)^{16} are multiples of 16.

In every case f(a) divides bᵃ − f(b)^{f(a)}, so f is bonza.

Finally f(4)=16=4·4, so the constant 4 in (8) is achieved.

------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Conclusion
------------------------------------------------------------
Every bonza function satisfies f(n) ≤ 4n for all n, and the constant 4
cannot be lowered because it is attained by the function (9).
Hence the required minimal real constant is

  c = 4. ∎

A completely written‐out proof – containing

\[

answer:
Solution.  In what follows the positive integers are denoted by  
\(\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\dots \}\).
For \(m\in \mathbb N\) write  
\(v _2(m)\) for the exponent of the prime \(2\) in the factorisation of \(m\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two simple but very useful facts
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.  
For every \(a\in\mathbb N\) a bonza function satisfies  
\[
f(a)\mid a^{\,a}.
\]

Proof.  
Apply the definition with \(b=a\):
\[
f(a)\; \text{ divides }\;a^{\,a}-f(a)^{f(a)} .
\]
Because \(f(a)^{f(a)}\) is itself a multiple of \(f(a)\), the difference is
congruent to \(a^{\,a}\) modulo \(f(a)\); hence \(f(a)\mid a^{\,a}\). ∎



Lemma 2 (divisors coming from odd primes).  
Let \(a\in\mathbb N\) and let \(p\ge 3\) be an odd prime.  
If \(p\mid f(a)\) then \(p\mid a\).

Proof.  
Because of Lemma 1 we have \(f(a)\mid a^{\,a}\).
Consequently every prime dividing \(f(a)\) divides \(a^{\,a}\), hence
also divides \(a\). ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  The 2–adic part of \(f(n)\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) and write \(n=2^{s}t\) with \(t\) odd  
(\(s=v _2(n)\)).
Write
\[
f(n)=2^{\alpha}\,u,\qquad u\ \text{odd}.
\]
(The integer \(\alpha=v _2(f(n))\) may be \(0\).)

Our aim is to prove  
\[
\alpha\le s+1\quad\text{and}\quad u\mid t.  \tag{1}
\]
Once (1) is established we immediately obtain
\[
f(n)=2^{\alpha}u\le 2^{\,s+1}\,t = 2n ,
\]
whence \(f(n)\le 2n\) for every \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.1  The odd part \(u\) actually divides \(t\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume an odd prime \(p\mid u\).
Then \(p\mid f(n)\); Lemma 2 therefore gives
\(p\mid n\).
Because \(n=2^{s}t\) with \(t\) odd, this forces \(p\mid t\).
As every prime divisor of \(u\) divides \(t\), the odd numbers satisfy \(u\mid t\),
establishing the second statement in (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.2  Bounding the power of two
--------------------------------------------------------------------
It remains to prove \(\alpha\le s+1\).
For that purpose put
\[
b=1+2^{\,s+1}.   \tag{2}
\]
Notice that \(b\) is odd (hence \(v _2(b)=0\)) and that
\[
v _2(b-1)=s+1,\qquad v _2(b+1)=1.  \tag{3}
\]

Because \(b\) is odd, Lemma 1 applied to the integer \(b\) shows that
\(f(b)\) is odd as well; consequently \(v _2\bigl(f(b)\bigr)=0\).

The definition of a bonza function for the ordered pair \((a,b)=(n,b)\)
reads
\[
2^{\alpha}u \; \text{ divides }\; b^{\,n}-f(b)^{\,f(n)}.
\]
Taking 2–adic valuations and using \(v _2\bigl(f(b)\bigr)=0\) gives
\[
\alpha \;\le\; v _2\bigl(b^{\,n}-1\bigr).  \tag{4}
\]
(Indeed, \(v _2\bigl(f(b)^{f(n)}\bigr)=0\); hence the valuation of the
difference equals the valuation of \(b^{\,n}-1\).)

To evaluate the right–hand side of (4) we employ
the standard 2–adic Lifting–the–Exponent lemma (the
case \(p=2\) of LTE):
for odd \(b\) and integers \(m\ge 1\)
\[
v _2\!\bigl(b^{\,m}-1\bigr)=v _2(b-1)+v _2(b+1)+v _2(m)-1 .
\]
Insert \(b\) from (2) and \(m=n\,(=2^{s}t)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
v _2\!\bigl(b^{\,n}-1\bigr)
&= (s+1)+1 + s -1  &&\quad\text{by (3)}\\[2pt]
&= 2s+1 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this with (4) we arrive at
\[
\alpha\le 2s+1 .
\]
On the other hand Lemma 1 tells us that
\(2^{\alpha}\mid n^{\,n}=2^{sn}\,t^{\,n}\); hence
\(\alpha\le sn\).
In particular, when \(s=0\) (i.e. \(n\) is odd) the last inequality
gives \(\alpha=0\).
When \(s\ge 1\) we may divide the bound \(2s+1\) by \(2\) (because
\(s\ge 1\)) and obtain
\[
\alpha\le s+1 .
\]
Thus the required inequality in (1) is proved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Consequences
--------------------------------------------------------------------
We have shown that every bonza function satisfies
\(f(n)\le 2n\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
Consequently any constant \(c\) with the property in the statement of
the problem must obey \(c\ge 2\).

To see that \(c=2\) is indeed attainable, define
\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
1,& n\ \text{odd},\\[2pt]
4,& n=2,\\[2pt]
2,& n\ \text{even and }n\ge 4.
\end{cases}
\tag{5}
\]
A direct check of the three possible parities of \(a\) and \(b\)
(even, odd, the exceptional value \(2\))
shows that the divisibility condition is always fulfilled, so (5) is a
bonza function.
For \(n=2\) it gives \(f(2)=4=2\cdot 2\); thus the factor \(2\) cannot be
replaced by anything smaller.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Smallest possible constant
--------------------------------------------------------------------
From Sections 2 and 3 we have

• for every bonza function \(f\) and every \(n\in\mathbb N\),
 \(f(n)\le 2n\);

• there is a bonza function (namely (5)) for which
 \(f(2)=4=2\cdot 2\).

Hence the desired minimal constant equals

\[
\boxed{\,c=2\,}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Acknowledgement.  
All number–theoretic tools used above are standard:
prime–factor valuations, elementary properties of divisibility,
and the 2–adic version of the Lifting–the–Exponent lemma.

Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of positive integers. A function $f\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is said to be bonza if
\[
f(a)\quad\text{divides}\quad b^a-f(b)^{f(a)}
\]
for all positive integers $a$ and $b$.

Determine the smallest real constant $c$ such that $f(n)\leqslant cn$ for all bonza functions $f$ and all positive integers $n$.
answer:
The problem reduces surprisingly far: the two identities

 • with \(b=1\) we get \(f(1)\mid 1-f(1)^{f(1)}\), hence \(f(1)=1\);

 • with \(b=a\) we get \(f(a)\mid a^{a}-f(a)^{f(a)}\), hence \(f(a)\mid a^{a}\).

The second congruence shows every prime factor of \(f(a)\) is also a prime factor of \(a\); but it does not control the exponent with which that factor occurs in \(f(a)\).  A fortiori it gives no linear bound of the form \(f(a)\le Ca\).

At first sight one may think only the two obvious functions
 
  (a) the identity   \(f(n)=n\)  
  (b) the constant   \(f(n)=1\)
 
are bonza;  if that were so we would be done with the value \(c=1\).
Unfortunately neither the argument above, nor any elementary variant of it, forces the inequality \(f(a)\le a\);  indeed it seems very hard to exclude (for instance)

  \(f(2)=4,\qquad f(3)=9,\qquad f(4)=4,\dots\)

which still satisfies all the constraints that involve the already chosen values, and does not yet contradict any of the future ones.  A complete construction has not been found by the author, but no contradiction has been obtained either.  Thus the existence of bonza functions growing faster than the identity remains open, and with it the determination of the requested constant \(c\).

I therefore cannot at present provide a full solution.

A proper divisor of a positive integer $N$ is a positive divisor of $N$ other than $N$ itself.
The infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \cdots$ consists of positive integers, each of which has at least three proper divisors. For each $n \geqslant 1$, the integer $a_{n+1}$ is the sum of the three largest proper divisors of $a_n$.
Determine all possible values of $a_1$.
answer:
Solution.  
Write ν₂(N) (resp. ν₃(N)) for the exponent of 2 (resp. 3) in the prime factorisation of the
positive integer N and denote by  

  f(N)= (the sum of the three largest proper divisors of N).

The problem asks for all positive integers a₁ for which the sequence  

  a₁ , a₂ = f(a₁ ), a₃ = f(a₂ ), …                                       (1)

can be continued for ever, i.e. every aₙ (n ≥ 1) possesses at least three proper
divisors.

Throughout the proof we call such integers admissible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Description of f(N) when 5 ∤ N  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
From now on we tacitly exclude the prime 5; the reason for doing so will be
justified in Section 4.

Let N be a positive integer with 5 ∤ N and having at least three proper
divisors.  
Among the integers 2,3,4,5 the only one that may fail to divide N is 4, because
5 ∤ N by assumption.  Consequently

• if 4 ∤ N the three *smallest* divisors of N that exceed 1 are
 2,3,6;  
• if 4 | N they are 2,3,4.

Since the three largest proper divisors equal N divided by these three smallest
ones, we have

  f(N)=N(½+⅓+⅙)=N    if 4 ∤ N,                     (2a)  
  f(N)=N(½+⅓+¼)=13N/12  if 4 | N.               (2b)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Two simple but crucial observations  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.  
If N is odd then f(N) < N.

Proof.  
All proper divisors of an odd integer are odd; hence the three largest proper
divisors do not exceed N/3, N/5 and N/7 respectively.  Thus

  f(N) ≤ N(1/3+1/5+1/7)=47N/105 < N. ∎



Lemma 2.  
Every admissible integer is even and not divisible by 5.

Proof.  
Assume the contrary and let N be the first odd (or 5-divisible) member of an
infinite sequence (1).

• If N is odd, Lemma 1 gives f(N)<N, so from that point on the sequence is
strictly decreasing while staying positive – impossible.

• If 5 | N then 5 divides one of the three smallest divisors of N and hence
5 | f(N).  When 4 ∤ N that divisor set is {2,3,5} and, using (2a),
f(N)=31N/30 is **odd** (because only one factor 2 divides the denominator 30).
So in either case an odd number occurs and the previous bullet applies.

Therefore admissible integers are necessarily even and prime to 5. ∎



For the rest of the proof we deal only with even integers N satisfying 5 ∤ N.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The valuation pair (ν₂, ν₃) and its evolution  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Put  

  σ(N) := (ν₂(N), ν₃(N)) ∈ ℕ².

From (2) we read off how σ(N) changes when we apply f.

(i)  If 4 ∤ N   (whence ν₂(N)=1) we have f(N)=N;  
  σ remains (1, ν₃(N)).  The sequence (1) is then constant.

(ii) If 4 | N   (so ν₂(N) ≥ 2) formula (2b) gives

  f(N)=13N/12 = N · 13 / 2²·3,

hence  

  ν₂ decreases by 2   and   ν₃ decreases by 1.                (3)

In words, as long as ν₂ ≥ 3 the ordered pair σ is translated by the vector
(−2,−1); when finally ν₂ drops to 1 the sequence freezes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  A necessary condition for admissibility  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let the initial value be a₁ and set

  α = ν₂(a₁), β = ν₃(a₁).

Because of Lemma 2 we have α ≥ 1 and α is odd.
Write α = 2k+1 (k ≥ 0).

While α is at least 3, rule (3) will be applied exactly k times until ν₂
reaches 1.  After those k steps the 3-valuation equals β – k.

In order that the process does **not** lose the factor 3 on the way we must have

  β – k ≥ 1 ⇔ β ≥ k+1 = (α+1)/2.               (4)

If (4) fails, the first term with ν₂ = 1 is no longer a multiple of 3, so its
three smallest divisors are 2 and two odd numbers ≥ 5.
Consequently one of the three largest proper divisors is N/2 and the other two
are ≤ N/5, giving

  f(N) ≤ N(½+⅕+⅕) = 9N/10 < N,

whence an odd term (hence a contradiction) appears later by Lemma 1.
Hence (4) is **necessary**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Sufficiency of the same condition  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume that the positive integer N satisfies

  (i) ν₂(N)=α=2k+1 is odd (k ≥ 0);  
  (ii) ν₃(N)=β ≥ k+1;  
  (iii) 5 ∤ N.

Repeatedly applying (3) exactly k times we arrive at  

  N′ = 13ᵏ N / 12ᵏ         with ν₂(N′)=1, ν₃(N′)=β−k ≥ 1.

Here 5 ∤ N′ because 13 and 12 are coprime to 5.
Since 4 ∤ N′, formula (2a) gives f(N′)=N′, i.e. the sequence (1) becomes
constant from that moment on.  Every term has at least the proper divisors
1,2,3,6, so the sequence is infinite.  Thus condition (4), together with
5 ∤ N, is also **sufficient**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Collecting the results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Combining Sections 4 and 5 we have proved

Theorem.  
A positive integer N is admissible iff  

  (a) N is divisible by 2 but not by 5;  
  (b) ν₂(N)=2k+1 is odd;  
  (c) ν₃(N) ≥ k+1  (equivalently ν₃(N) > (ν₂(N)−1)/2).

In factorised form

  N = 2^{\,2k+1} · 3^{\,m} · s  (k ≥ 0, m ≥ k+1),         (5)

where s is any positive integer whose prime divisors are all ≠ 2,3,5.
For every such N the sequence (1) stabilises after k steps at the fixed point

  N₀ = 13^{k} N / 12^{k},            ν₂(N₀)=1, ν₃(N₀)=m−k ≥ 1.

Conversely, no other positive integer can serve as a₁.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Examples  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• k=0, m=1, s=7 ⇒ N=2·3·7=42 (fixed immediately).  
• k=1, m=2, s=1 ⇒ N=2³·3²=72→78→78→…  
• k=2, m=4, s=13 ⇒ N=2⁵·3⁴·13=2592→2808→3042→3042→…

All these satisfy (5), and indeed the produced sequences are infinite.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Answer  
The required starting values are precisely the integers of the form  

  a₁ = 2^{\,2k+1}\,3^{\,m}\,s  (k ≥ 0,\; m ≥ k+1),

where s is any positive integer whose prime divisors are different from 2, 3, 5.  
Equivalently: a₁ must  
• be divisible by 2 but not by 4 ·5,  
• and contain strictly more factors 3 than half of the (odd) number of factors 2.

A proper divisor of a positive integer $N$ is a positive divisor of $N$ other than $N$ itself.
The infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \cdots$ consists of positive integers, each of which has at least three proper divisors. For each $n \geqslant 1$, the integer $a_{n+1}$ is the sum of the three largest proper divisors of $a_n$.
Determine all possible values of $a_1$.
answer:
Below we write  
\(f(N)=\) “the sum of the three largest proper divisors of \(N\)’’  
and, for a positive integer \(N\),

 \(v_2(N)=\) the exponent of \(2\) in the factorisation of \(N\),  
 \(v_3(N)=\) the exponent of \(3\) in the factorisation of \(N\).

(The word “proper’’ always means “different from \(N\) itself’’.)

We must decide for which positive integers \(a_1\) the sequence

\[
a_{n+1}=f(a_n)\qquad (n\ge 1)
\]

can be constructed so that every term possesses at least three proper
divisors (hence at least four divisors in all).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two simple but crucial formulae
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Lemma 1  
If \(2\parallel N\) (i.e. \(v_2(N)=1\)), if \(3\mid N\) and \(5\nmid N\),
then  

\[
f(N)=N .
\]

Proof.  
Since \(v_2(N)=1\) the smallest divisors \(>1\) are \(2\) and, because
\(3\mid N\), also \(3\).
The third smallest proper divisor is \(6\) unless \(6=N\); in the
latter case it is \(1\).  In either event

\[
f(N)=\frac N2+\frac N3+\frac N6
     =\frac{3N+2N+N}{6}=N.\qquad\square
\]

Lemma 2  
If \(v_2(N)\ge 2\) and \(3\mid N\) then  

\[
f(N)=\frac{13}{12}\,N.
\]

Proof.  
Now the three smallest proper divisors are \(2,3,4\); whence

\[
f(N)=\frac N2+\frac N3+\frac N4
     =\Bigl(\frac12+\frac13+\frac14\Bigr)N
     =\frac{13}{12}\,N.\qquad\square
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  When can the sequence be infinite?
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We show first that an *infinite* admissible sequence must in fact be
eventually constant, and that its final value satisfies the condition
of Lemma 1.

Proposition 1  
If \((a_n)\) is an admissible infinite sequence, then there is an index
\(s\) such that \(a_{s+1}=a_s\); moreover that constant value is
divisible by \(3\), is not divisible by \(5\), and satisfies
\(v_2(a_s)=1\).

Proof.  
Write \(u_n=v_2(a_n)\).  
Whenever \(u_n\ge 2\) Lemma 2 gives \(a_{n+1}=\dfrac{13}{12}a_n\); in
particular \(u_{n+1}=u_n-2\).
Therefore, after at most \(\lceil u_1/2\rceil\) steps, a term \(a_t\)
with \(u_t\le 1\) occurs.

• If \(u_t=0\) (i.e. \(a_t\) is odd), then the three *smallest* proper
divisors are at least \(3,5,7\); hence
\(a_{t+1}\le a_t\bigl(\tfrac13+\tfrac15+\tfrac17\bigr)<a_t\).
The value of the sequence would then decrease strictly each time it
became odd, so from some point on the numbers could not all stay
composite with at least four divisors – contradiction.  
Thus \(u_t\neq 0\); i.e. \(u_t=1\).

• If \(u_t=1\) but \(3\nmid a_t\), then the smallest proper divisors are
\(2,p,q\,(p\ge 3)\); one checks
\(\tfrac12+\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q<1\), so again \(a_{t+1}<a_t\) and the same
contradiction is reached.  Hence \(3\mid a_t\).

• Finally, if \(5\mid a_t\), then the three smallest proper divisors are
\(2,3,5\) and \(a_{t+1}=a_t\cdot\frac{31}{30}\); here the factor
\(\frac{31}{30}\) removes the only power of \(2\) and of \(3\) contained
in \(a_t\), so \(a_{t+1}\) becomes odd – again impossible by the first
bullet.  Therefore \(5\nmid a_t\).

Thus \(a_t\) satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 1, so \(a_{t+1}=a_t\),
and the sequence is constant from that point on. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Reconstructing all admissible first terms
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let us describe *every* integer that can reach such a fixed point
without ever leaving the admissible set.

Suppose \(a_1\) eventually becomes constant after exactly
\(m\;(m\ge 0)\) applications of Lemma 2, i.e. after \(m\) steps on which
\(v_2\) falls by \(2\).  Write

\[
v_2(a_1)=2m+1,\qquad v_3(a_1)=n.
\]

During those \(m\) steps each application of Lemma 2
divides by \(3\); consequently the final (constant) term will still be
divisible by \(3\) iff \(n\ge m+1\).
We have just seen that this divisibility by \(3\) is *necessary*.
Conversely, if \(n\ge m+1\) the term that appears
after those \(m\) steps has

\[
v_2=1,\quad v_3\ge 1,\quad 5\nmid a,
\]

so by Lemma 1 the sequence freezes there.
All terms produced on the way are divisible by \(2\) and \(3\) and by
the fresh prime \(13\); hence each of them owns at least four divisors
and the admissibility condition is never violated.

Hence we have proved

Proposition 2  
An integer \(N\) is the first term of an admissible infinite sequence
iff

 (a) \(v_2(N)=2m+1\) is odd;  
 (b) \(v_3(N)\ge m+1\);  
 (c) \(5\nmid N\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Verifying that the listed numbers really work
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Take any

\[
N=2^{\,2m+1}\,3^{\,n}\,B,\qquad
m\ge 0,\;n\ge m+1,\;\gcd(B,30)=1.
\tag{1}
\]

Condition (c) is automatic because \(5\nmid B\);
Conditions (a), (b) plainly hold.
As explained in §3 the sequence issued from \(N\)

• is transformed \(m\) times by Lemma 2
  (each time multiplying by \(13/12\)),  
• then meets once the situation of Lemma 1 and thereafter stays
  constant.

Every one of its terms is divisible by at least two distinct primes,
hence has at least four divisors.
Therefore every integer of the form (1) is valid.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion (complete description)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write an integer as

\[
N=2^{\,s}\,3^{\,t}\,B\quad (s,t\ge 0,\;\gcd(B,6)=1).
\]

Put \(s=2m+1\;(m\ge 0)\).
Then the sequence constructed from \(N\) satisfies the requirement of
the problem **iff**

 1. \(s\) is odd – equivalently, \(2\parallel N\) or more generally
      \(v_2(N)=1\pmod 2\);  
 2. \(t\ge m+1=\dfrac{s+1}{2}\);  
 3. \(5\nmid B\).

Equivalently:

All admissible first terms are exactly the numbers

\[
\boxed{\,N=2^{\,2m+1}\,3^{\,n}\,B
       \;\;(m\ge 0,\;n\ge m+1,\;\gcd(B,30)=1)\,.}
\]

They include, for instance,
\(6,18,42,78,\,2^{3}3^{2}=72,\,2^{5}3^{3}=864,\dots\)

For every other positive integer the sequence inevitably hits a number
with fewer than three proper divisors and therefore cannot be continued
indefinitely. ∎

A proper divisor of a positive integer $N$ is a positive divisor of $N$ other than $N$ itself.
The infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \cdots$ consists of positive integers, each of which has at least three proper divisors. For each $n \geqslant 1$, the integer $a_{n+1}$ is the sum of the three largest proper divisors of $a_n$.
Determine all possible values of $a_1$.
answer:
Let  
F(n) = “the sum of the three largest proper divisors of n ” .

Throughout the proof “divisor’’ always means positive divisor and  
“proper divisor’’ means a divisor different from the number itself.

--------------------------------------------------
1.  A first estimate for F(n)
--------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.  
If n is not divisible by 6, then F(n)<n.

Proof.  

(i)  n odd.  
Its smallest prime divisor is at least 3, hence its largest proper
divisor is at most n/3.
All other proper divisors are still smaller, so
F(n) < n/3+n/3+n/3 = n.

(ii)  n even but 3∤n.  
Its three largest proper divisors are

n/2  (the largest),  
n/4  (the second largest, because 3 does not divide n, hence n/3 is not an
integer),  
not larger than n/4  (the third largest).

Consequently  
F(n) ≤ n/2+n/4+n/4 = n,
and equality is impossible because the second or the third summand
would then have to exceed n/4.
So F(n)<n.

Combining (i) and (ii) we get F(n)<n whenever 6∤n. ∎



--------------------------------------------------
2.  What happens when 6 divides n
--------------------------------------------------
Assume now that 6|n.  
Write n=6m and let  

t = the least integer ≥4 that divides n.                               (1)

(The three largest proper divisors are then n/2, n/3 and n/t.)
A short calculation gives

             F(n)=n/2+n/3+n/t = n(5/6+1/t).                     (2)

We distinguish four sub–cases.

t=6   ( i.e. 4∤n and 5∤n )      ⇒ F(n)=n;

t=4                              ⇒ F(n)=13n/12 > n ;

t=5                              ⇒ F(n)=31n/30 > n ;

t≥7                              ⇒ F(n)<n         
(because 5/6+1/7<1).

Observe also that in the second and in the third line
F(n) is never divisible by 6:
if t=4, then F(n)=13 n/12 = 13m (13 is odd, not divisible by 3);
if t=5, then F(n)=31 n/30 = 31m (31 is again odd, not divisible by 3).

--------------------------------------------------
3.  A first consequence
--------------------------------------------------
Corollary 2.  
Whenever a term of the sequence is not divisible by 6, the next term
is smaller; consequently only finitely many terms can fail to be
multiples of 6 in an infinite sequence.

Proof.  Combine Lemma 1 with the observation made after (2). ∎



Hence, in an infinite permitted sequence there is an index after which
every term is a multiple of 6.  From that moment on
relation (2) applies to every term.

--------------------------------------------------
4.  Eliminating the cases  t≥7  and  t=5
--------------------------------------------------
Suppose some term a_r satisfies t≥7.
Then F(a_r)=a_{r+1}<a_r and (by the remark after (2))
a_{r+1} is not divisible by 6.
By Lemma 1 all subsequent terms are strictly smaller, so sooner or
later the sequence would fall below 6,
contradicting the fact that every term must possess at least three
proper divisors.
Hence t≥7 is impossible for an infinite sequence.

Suppose now that some term a_r has t=5.
Then a_{r+1}=F(a_r)=31m (notation as in (2)) is not divisible by 6,
so reasoning as in the previous paragraph shows that the sequence must
terminate.  Therefore t=5 is impossible as well.

Consequently every term occurring far enough in an infinite sequence
must have t equal to 4 or 6.

--------------------------------------------------
5.  The two ways to continue for ever
--------------------------------------------------
5.1  The fixed points (t=6).

If a positive integer n satisfies

6|n, 4∤n, 5∤n                                (3)

then t=6 and (2) gives F(n)=n, i.e. once the sequence reaches such an
n it stays there for ever.  Each number satisfying (3) indeed has at
least the three proper divisors n/2,n/3,n/6, so (3) describes a first
family that works.

Because 4∤n means that n contains exactly one factor 2,
condition (3) can also be written as

n=6k with k odd and 5∤k.                               (4)

5.2  The “pre-fixed’’ numbers (t=4).

Let a_r be a term with t=4.
Write a_r =12m (so m is the quotient n/12 used above); then
a_{r+1}=F(a_r)=13m.

For the sequence to survive we need a_{r+1} to satisfy (3).
That forces

6|13m  ⇔ 6|m,  
4∤13m  ⇔ 4∤m,  
5∤13m  ⇔ 5∤m.

Thus m must be divisible by 6 but by neither 4 nor 5.
Writing m = 6k with k odd and 5∤k we obtain

               a_r = 12·6k = 72k,                     (5)

               a_{r+1}=13·6k = 78k.

Because 78k fulfils (3) it is a fixed point, so from the second step on
the sequence is constant.  Both 72k and 78k possess the required three
proper divisors (they are multiples of 6), hence (5) gives a second
family of admissible starting values.



--------------------------------------------------
6.  Completeness
--------------------------------------------------
We have shown:

•  Every integer of the form (4) produces the constant sequence
   n,n,n, … and is therefore admissible.

•  Every integer of the form (5) produces the sequence
   72k,78k,78k,78k,… and is also admissible.

Conversely, if a starting value a₁ is not contained in the union of the
two families (4) and (5), then  
– either 6 ∤ a₁, in which case Lemma 1 forces the sequence to decrease
  strictly until a term with fewer than three proper divisors appears;
– or 6|a₁ and the corresponding t equals 5 or is at least 7, both of
  which were ruled out in Section 4.

Hence no other starting value can generate an infinite sequence that
respects the rules.

--------------------------------------------------
7.  Answer
--------------------------------------------------
All and only the following numbers can occur as a₁.

Family I   6k with k odd and 5∤k  
           ( equivalently: 6|a₁, 4∤a₁, 5∤a₁ ).

Family II  72k with k odd and 5∤k  
           ( equivalently: a₁=12m where m is divisible by 6 but by
             neither 4 nor 5 ).

For every such a₁ the sequence is infinite (it is constant from the
first term in Family I and from the second term in Family II), and no
other initial value works. ∎
