A proper divisor of a positive integer $N$ is a positive divisor of $N$ other than $N$ itself.
The infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \cdots$ consists of positive integers, each of which has at least three proper divisors. For each $n \geqslant 1$, the integer $a_{n+1}$ is the sum of the three largest proper divisors of $a_n$.
Determine all possible values of $a_1$.
answer:
Solution.

For a positive integer \(n\) denote by  

\[
f(n)=\text {“sum of the three largest proper divisors of }n\text ” .
\]

We have \(a_{k+1}=f(a_{k})\;(k\ge 1)\).
Write \(v_{p}(n)\) for the exponent of the prime \(p\) in the factorisation of \(n\)
(\(p\)-adic valuation).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two useful lemmata
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.  
If \(4\mid n\) and \(3\mid n\) then the three largest proper divisors of \(n\) are
\(n/2,\;n/3,\;n/4\); consequently

\[
f(n)=\frac{n}{2}+\frac{n}{3}+\frac{n}{4}=\frac{13}{12}\,n .
\]

Proof.  
Because \(2\) is the smallest prime factor of \(n\), \(n/2\) is the largest
proper divisor.  
Since \(3\mid n\) while \(4\mid n\), one has \(n/3>n/4\); no other proper
divisor is larger than \(n/3\).  Finally \(n/4\) exceeds every divisor obtained
from \(n\) by dividing by a product of at least two odd primes or by \(8\).
∎



Lemma 2 (fixed points).  
Let \(n=6k\) with  
(i) \(k\) odd and  
(ii) \(5\nmid k\).
Then the three largest proper divisors of \(n\) are
\(3k,\;2k,\;k\) and hence \(f(n)=n\).

Proof.  
Because \(n=2\cdot 3\cdot k\,(k\text{ odd})\) the divisors \(3k\;(=n/2)\) and
\(2k\;(=n/3)\) are the two greatest proper divisors.

For every prime \(q\ge7\) dividing \(k\) one has
\[
\frac{n}{q}=\frac{6k}{q}\le\frac{6k}{7}<k,
\]
while the only even proper divisors below \(2k\) are
\(n/4=3k/2<k\).  
Because \(5\nmid k\) we are not obliged to compare with \(n/5\);
thus the third largest proper divisor is \(k\) itself and
\(f(n)=3k+2k+k=6k=n\). ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  How \(f\) changes the 2- and 3-adic orders
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 3.  
Suppose \(v_{2}(n)\ge 2\) and \(3\mid n\).
Put \(n_{1}=f(n)\).  Then  

\[
v_{2}(n_{1})=v_{2}(n)-2,\qquad
v_{3}(n_{1})=v_{3}(n)-1
\tag{1}
\]

and no new prime except possibly \(13\) is introduced.

Proof.  
By Lemma 1, \(n_{1}=13n/12\).
Because \(13\) is odd and \(12=2^{2}\!\cdot\! 3\),
formula (1) is immediate. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The numbers that work
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Write the prime factorisation of the candidate first term \(a_{1}\) as

\[
a_{1}=2^{\alpha}\,3^{\beta}\,m,\qquad
m\text{ odd},\;5\nmid m.
\tag{2}
\]

(The factor \(5\) is forbidden for the reason explained in §4.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.1  Sufficiency
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume  

\[
\alpha=2s+1\;\;(\text{odd}),\qquad
\beta\ge s+1.
\tag{3}
\]

Starting from \(a_{1}\) apply Lemma 3 exactly \(s\) times.
After the \(s\)-th step the exponent of \(2\) has fallen from
\(2s+1\) to \(1\), while the exponent of \(3\) has fallen from
\(\beta\) to at least \(\beta-s\ge 1\).
Hence

\[
a_{s+1}=2\cdot 3^{\beta-s}\,m\,13^{s}=6k
\quad\text{with }k\text{ odd and }5\nmid k .
\]

By Lemma 2 this term is a fixed point of \(f\); consequently the
sequence \((a_{n})\) is constant from the index \(s+1\) on, so all
its terms have (in fact exactly) three proper divisors.
Thus every \(a_{1}\) satisfying (2)–(3) indeed generates an admissible
infinite sequence.



--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.2  Necessity
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Now suppose that an integer \(a_{1}\) produces an admissible infinite
sequence; we prove that (2)–(3) must hold.

•  If \(\alpha\) is even, repeated use of Lemma 3 eventually eliminates
all factors \(2\); the first odd term that appears is smaller than its
predecessor (because the largest proper divisor of an odd
number is at most one third of the number), whence the sequence
strictly decreases from that point and cannot be infinite.
Hence \(\alpha\) is odd: \(\alpha=2s+1\,(s\ge 0)\).

•  During the first \(s\) applications of \(f\) the 3-adic order drops
by \(\!s\) (Lemma 3 again), so to prevent the factor \(3\) from
vanishing we must have \(\beta\ge s+1\); this is (3).

•  Finally assume \(5\mid m\).  Write \(a_{n}=6k\) for the first term
of the sequence that is divisible exactly once by \(2\).
Because \(5\mid k\) the divisor \(a_{n}/5=6k/5\) exceeds
\(k\), so the three largest proper divisors of \(a_{n}\) are
\(3k,2k,6k/5\).  Thus

\[
a_{n+1}=f(a_{n})=6k+\frac{k}{5}\;(>\!a_{n}),
\]
and \(a_{n+1}\) is odd.  For every odd number the sequence
strictly decreases (reason quoted above), so it must terminate, a
contradiction.  Hence \(5\nmid m\).

Therefore every admissible first term has the shape (2) with the
constraints (3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Combine §§3.1 and 3.2.

The set of all positive integers that can occur as \(a_{1}\) is

\[
\boxed{%
\bigl\{\,2^{\,2s+1}\,3^{\,t}\,m\;:\;
s,t\in\mathbb N_{0},\;t\ge s+1,\;
m\text{ odd},\;5\nmid m\bigr\}} .
\]

Equivalently:  
\(a_{1}\) must be divisible by \(2\) to an odd power, by \(3\) to at
least half that power plus one, and by no factor \(5\); these
conditions are also sufficient.

Every such \(a_{1}\) stabilises after exactly \(s\) steps at the fixed
value  

\[
6\,\bigl(3^{\,t-s}\,m\,13^{\,s}\bigr)
\]

whose odd part is not a multiple of \(5\).

Consider a $2025 \times 2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of different sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.
Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
answer:
Solution.  
Throughout the proof we write \(n=2025\).

1 Reformulation  
Because every row and every column has exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is of the form  
\[
\{(1,c_{1}),\,(2,c_{2}),\ldots ,(n,c_{n})\},
\]
where \(c_{1},c_{2},\ldots ,c_{n}\) are the numbers \(1,2,\ldots ,n\) in some order (indeed, in each row \(r\) we uncover the unique square in column \(c_{r}\), and because every column is uncovered exactly once the numbers \(c_{r}\) are all different).

Our task is to cover the remaining \(n(n-1)\) squares with pairwise disjoint axis–parallel rectangles (the “tiles”) and to determine the smallest possible number of tiles.

2 A universal lower bound of \(2n-2\)

For \(k=1,2,\dots ,n-1\) define the two squares  

\[
A_k=(k,\;c_{k+1})\qquad\text{and}\qquad
B_k=(k+1,\;c_{k}).
\]

(The column of \(A_k\) is the column that is left uncovered in the next row,
and the row of \(B_k\) is the row that is left uncovered in the previous
column.)  
None of the \(2n-2\) squares \(A_1,\dots ,A_{n-1},B_1,\dots ,B_{n-1}\) is
uncovered, because in row \(k\) the only uncovered square is \((k,c_{k})\),
while the column of \(A_k\) equals \(c_{k+1}\ne c_k\); the argument for the
\(B_k\) is analogous.

Lemma.  A single rectangular tile can contain at most one of the squares
\[
A_1,\dots ,A_{n-1},\;B_1,\dots ,B_{n-1}.
\]

Proof.  
Assume, to obtain a contradiction, that some tile \(R\) contains two of those
squares.  Because of symmetry we may distinguish four cases; we treat the
first and note that the other three are identical.

Case 1: \(R\) contains \(A_a\) and \(A_b\) with \(a<b\).
The two squares are

\[
A_a=(a,c_{a+1}),\qquad A_b=(b,c_{b+1}).
\]

Consequently the row–interval of \(R\) contains all rows from \(a\) to
\(b\), and its column–interval contains both \(c_{a+1}\) and
\(c_{b+1}\).  In particular \(R\) contains the square
\((a+1,c_{a+1})\); but this square is uncovered (it is the unique uncovered
square of row \(a+1\)), contradicting the definition of a tile.

Case 2: both squares are of type \(B\) is handled by swapping the roles of
rows and columns.

Case 3: \(R\) contains \(A_a\) and \(B_b\).  
If \(a\le b\) then, just as above, \(R\) contains row \(a+1\) and column
\(c_{a+1}\) and therefore contains the uncovered square
\((a+1,c_{a+1})\).  
If \(a>b\) we argue similarly with \(B_b\).

Case 4: \(R\) contains \(A_a\) and \(B_a\).
By definition \(A_a\) has coordinates \((a,c_{a+1})\) and \(B_a\)
coordinates \((a+1,c_{a})\).  The rectangle determined by those two points
has opposite vertices \((a,c_a)\) and \((a+1,c_{a+1})\); hence
\((a,c_a)\) – an uncovered square – lies inside \(R\), again a
contradiction.  ∎

Because every tile covers at most one of the \(2n-2\) special squares, at
least \(2n-2\) tiles are necessary:

\[
\boxed{\text{Number of tiles}\ge 2n-2}.
\]

For \(n=2025\) this lower bound equals \(4048\).

3 A construction that uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles  

It remains to show that \(2n-2\) tiles are in fact sufficient.  We do this
by exhibiting an explicit tiling.

Choose the uncovered squares to be the main diagonal,
\[
(1,1),(2,2),\ldots ,(n,n).
\]

(The choice is allowed, because it obviously meets the condition “one per
row and one per column”.)

Now use two families of rectangles.

Horizontal rectangles.  
For every row \(i\;(1\le i\le n-1)\) place a tile that covers the part of the
row to the right of its uncovered square, that is

\[
H_i=\{(i,j)\mid i+1\le j\le n\}.
\]

Each \(H_i\) is a \(1\times (n-i)\) rectangle and avoids the diagonal square
\((i,i)\).

Vertical rectangles.  
For every column \(j\;(1\le j\le n-1)\) place a tile that covers the part of
the column below its uncovered square,

\[
V_j=\{(k,j)\mid j+1\le k\le n\}.
\]

Each \(V_j\) is an \((n-j)\times 1\) rectangle and avoids the diagonal square
\((j,j)\).

Counting tiles.  
We placed \(n-1\) horizontal and \(n-1\) vertical rectangles, altogether
\(2n-2\) rectangles.

Verification.  
•  The horizontal rectangles lie strictly above the main diagonal, the
vertical rectangles lie strictly below it, so no two rectangles overlap.  
•  Together they cover every square except the \(n\) diagonal squares
(which were declared uncovered).  Hence they form a legitimate tiling.

Thus

\[
\boxed{\text{Number of tiles}\le 2n-2}.
\]

4 Conclusion  
The lower and upper bounds coincide, so the minimum possible number of tiles
is exactly \(2n-2\).

For \(n=2025\) this number is  

\[
2\cdot 2025-2=4048.
\]

Therefore Matilda needs at least, and can always manage with,  

\[
\boxed{4048\text{ tiles}.}
\]

Consider a $2025 \times 2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of different sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.
Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
answer:
Let \(n=2025\).
Throughout the proof we identify every unit square by the pair
\((r,c)\) of its row and column numbers (\(1\le r,c\le n\)).
For every row \(r\) let  
\(f(r)\;(1\le f(r)\le n)\) be the column that is *not* to be covered in that
row.  
Because every column also contains exactly one uncovered square,  
\(f\) is a permutation of \(\{1,2,\dots ,n\}\).

------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two families of compulsory squares
------------------------------------------------------------------
For every \(1\le i\le n-1\) define  

\[
A_i=(\,i,\;f(i+1)\,),\qquad  
B_i=(\,i+1,\;f(i)\,).
\]

None of these \(2(n-1)\) squares is uncovered, because
\(f(i)\neq f(i+1)\).
They will be called *special* squares.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A tile can contain at most one special square
------------------------------------------------------------------
Consider an arbitrary tile \(T\) (a rectangle of covered squares).

Lemma 1.  
If \(T\) contains \(A_i\) it cannot meet row \(i+1\); hence the bottom
edge of \(T\) lies on the grid line between rows \(i\) and \(i+1\).

Proof.  
\(A_i\) lies in column \(f(i+1)\).
If \(T\) also touched row \(i+1\) it would have to contain
\((i+1,f(i+1))\) as this square is in the same column and every
column-interval of a rectangle is the same in every row it meets.
But \((i+1,f(i+1))\) is *uncovered*, contradicting the rules.
\(\square\)

Lemma 2.  
If \(T\) contains \(B_i\) it cannot meet row \(i\); hence the top
edge of \(T\) lies on the grid line between rows \(i\) and \(i+1\).

(The proof is identical to that of Lemma 1, using the uncovered square
\((i,f(i))\).)

Corollary 1.  
Two distinct squares of the form \(A_i\) lie in different tiles
(because their bottom edges must be on different horizontal grid
lines).  
The same holds for the squares \(B_i\).

Lemma 3.  
No tile contains one square of type \(A\) and another of type \(B\).

Proof.  
Assume \(T\) contained \(A_i\) and \(B_j\) with \(i\le j\).
Then \(T\) meets rows \(i\) and \(j+1\); hence it also meets row
\(j\).
Column \(f(j)\) is part of \(T\) (it contains \(B_j\)), so
\((j,f(j))\) would be in \(T\).  But this square is uncovered, a
contradiction. \(\square\)

From Lemma 3 and Corollary 1 we deduce

Corollary 2.  
Each tile contains *at most one* special square.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The lower bound
------------------------------------------------------------------
There are exactly \(2(n-1)=4048\) special squares, and no tile can
contain more than one of them.  Hence every tiling that satisfies
Matilda’s requirements uses

\[
\boxed{\,2(n-1)=4048\,}
\]

tiles or more.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  A tiling with 4048 tiles
------------------------------------------------------------------
Choose the uncovered squares to be the main diagonal,
\((r,r)\;(1\le r\le n)\).

For every \(r=1,2,\dots ,n-1\) place  
a horizontal \(1\times(n-r)\) tile covering the squares
\[
(r,\;r+1),\,(r,\;r+2),\dots ,(r,n)
\]
(the part of row \(r\) to the right of the diagonal).

For every \(r=2,3,\dots ,n\) place  
a horizontal \(1\times(r-1)\) tile covering
\[
(r,\;1),\,(r,\;2),\dots ,(r,r-1)
\]
(the part of row \(r\) to the left of the diagonal).

These two families give \((n-1)+(n-1)=2(n-1)=4048\) disjoint
rectangular tiles; together with the \(n\) diagonal holes they cover
every square exactly once or not at all, and each row and column has
precisely one uncovered square.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion
------------------------------------------------------------------
Both the lower bound and the construction show that Matilda cannot do
better and can indeed achieve the bound, so the minimum possible
number of tiles is

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

Throughout we denote by \(n\) the side–length of the board (in our problem
\(n=2025\)).
Thus we work with an \(n\times n\) array of unit squares.
Exactly one square in every row and in every column has to be
left uncovered; these uncovered squares will be called
holes.

Our aim is to determine the least possible number \(t(n)\) of
rectangular tiles whose sides lie on grid–lines,
that can be placed so that

• no tile overlaps another one,  
• no tile covers a hole,  
• every row and every column contains precisely one hole.

We shall prove

\[
t(n)=2n-2\qquad (n\ge 1).
\]

For \(n=2025\) this gives \(t(2025)=4048\).

The proof is split into two parts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A construction with \(2n-2\) tiles (upper bound)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Place the holes on the main diagonal, i.e.
row \(i\) contains the hole in column \(i\)
for each \(1\le i\le n\).
(An illustration for \(n=6\) is given on the right-hand side.)

Cover the remaining squares as follows.

Horizontal rectangles  
for every \(i=1,2,\dots ,n-1\):
\[
H_i=\{(i,j)\mid j=i+1,i+2,\dots ,n\},
\]
i.e. all squares that lie to the right of the hole in row \(i\).

Vertical rectangles  
for every \(i=1,2,\dots ,n-1\):
\[
V_i=\{(j,i)\mid j=i+1,i+2,\dots ,n\},
\]
i.e. all squares that lie below the hole in column \(i\).

•  Each \(H_i\) and each \(V_j\) is a
rectangular block whose sides are on grid-lines.

•  Two different horizontal rectangles lie in different rows, hence
are disjoint; two different vertical rectangles lie in different
columns, hence are disjoint; finally a horizontal rectangle lies
strictly above the main diagonal whereas a vertical rectangle lies
strictly below it, so a horizontal and a vertical rectangle are also
disjoint.  Thus the \(2(n-1)\) rectangles do not overlap.

•  Every square of the board is either on the diagonal (and therefore
a hole) or is situated strictly above or strictly below it, hence it
belongs to exactly one of our rectangles.

Hence we have found a legal tiling
with \(2(n-1)\) rectangles, i.e.

\[
t(n)\le 2n-2. \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A lower bound of \(2n-2\) tiles
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let an arbitrary legal tiling be given and
let the hole in row \(i\) be situated in column
\(h_i\;(1\le h_i\le n)\).
Because there is also exactly one hole in every column,
all numbers \(h_1,h_2,\dots ,h_n\) are distinct;
they form a permutation of \(\{1,2,\dots ,n\}\).

For every \(i=1,2,\dots ,n-1\) we look at the two
covered squares

\[
A_i=(\,i,\;h_{\,i+1}\,),\qquad
B_i=(\,i+1,\;h_{\,i}\,).
\]

(The indices are chosen so that neither \(A_i\) nor \(B_i\) is a hole:
row \(i\) contains its hole in column \(h_i\ne h_{i+1}\), and
column \(h_i\) contains its hole in row \(i\), not in row \(i+1\), etc.)

Let \(R_i\) be the tile that covers \(A_i\) and
\(S_i\) the tile that covers \(B_i\).

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.   The tile \(R_i\) contains no square of row \(i+1\);
equivalently, its bottom edge lies on the grid–line between rows
\(i\) and \(i+1\).

Proof.  
\(A_i\) lies in column \(h_{\,i+1}\).
Assume \(R_i\) also covered a square in row \(i+1\);
then row \(i+1\) belongs to \(R_i\) and so does
column \(h_{\,i+1}\) (because \(A_i\) is in that column),
hence the hole \((\,i+1,h_{\,i+1})\) would be inside \(R_i\),
contradicting that holes are not covered.
∎

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 2.   The tile \(S_i\) contains no square of row \(i\);
equivalently, its top edge lies on the grid–line between rows
\(i\) and \(i+1\).

(The proof is identical with the one for Lemma 1.)

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 3.   All the \(2(n-1)\) tiles
\(R_1,R_2,\dots ,R_{n-1},S_1,S_2,\dots ,S_{n-1}\)
are pairwise different.

Proof.  
•  Lemma 1 shows that the bottom edge of \(R_i\) is the
line between rows \(i\) and \(i+1\).
For different indices \(i\neq j\) these bottom edges lie on
different horizontal grid–lines, so \(R_i\neq R_j\).

•  Lemma 2 shows that the top edge of \(S_i\)
is the same horizontal line,
and again two different indices give two different tiles.

•  A tile cannot be both some \(R_i\) and some \(S_j\) because
its bottom edge would then be between rows \(i\) and \(i+1\)
while its top edge would be between rows \(j\!+\!1\) and
\(j\!+\!2\); a single rectangle cannot possess two different
top (or bottom) edges.
∎

----------------------------------------------------------------
Corollary.   Every legal tiling uses at least \(2(n-1)\) tiles, i.e.

\[
t(n)\ge 2n-2. \tag{2}
\]

Indeed, Lemma 3 produces \(2(n-1)\) distinct tiles that must all be
present in any tiling.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The upper bound (1) and the lower bound (2) coincide, therefore

\[
t(n)=2n-2\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 1.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The required number for the given board
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(n=2025\) we obtain

\[
t(2025)=2\cdot 2025-2=4048.
\]

Hence Matilda cannot manage with fewer than \(4048\) rectangular tiles,
and the construction of Section 1 shows that \(4048\) tiles do suffice.
Therefore the minimum number of tiles is

\[
\boxed{\,4048\,}.
\]

problem:
Consider a $2025 \times 2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of different sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.
Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.

Consider a $2025 \times 2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of different sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.
Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
answer:
Let \(n=2025\) and, more generally, let us work with an arbitrary integer \(n\ge 2\).
(The case \(n=1\) is trivial – the only unit square must be left uncovered,
so zero tiles are needed.)

We shall prove the following statement.

Claim.  
For any \(n\times n\) board with one uncovered unit square in every row
and every column

 (a) at least \(2n-2\) rectangular tiles are necessary, and  

 (b) \(2n-2\) tiles are always sufficient.

Consequently the required minimum for the \(2025\times 2025\) board is

\[
2\cdot 2025-2=4048.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A lower bound of \(2n-2\).

Label the unique uncovered square in row \(i\) by \((i,\pi(i))\);
thus \(\pi\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

For every row \(i\) with \(\pi(i)\ge 2\) let  

\[
L_i=(i,\pi(i)-1)
\]

be the unit square immediately to the left of the hole.
Analogously, for every row \(i\) with \(\pi(i)\le n-1\) let  

\[
R_i=(i,\pi(i)+1)
\]

be the unit square immediately to its right.
(If the hole is in the first column there is no \(L_i\);  
if it is in the last column there is no \(R_i\).)

Counting.  
Because each column \(2,3,\dots ,n\) contains exactly one hole, every
such column contributes one and only one left–neighbour square.
Hence

\[
\bigl|\{\,L_i\}\bigr| = n-1 .
\]

Similarly, each column \(1,2,\dots ,n-1\) produces exactly
one right–neighbour square, so

\[
\bigl|\{\,R_i\}\bigr| = n-1 .
\]

Altogether there are \(2n-2\) distinguished squares of the kinds
\(L_i\) and \(R_i\).

Key observation.  
No single tile can contain more than one of these distinguished squares.

•  Two left–neighbour squares cannot lie in the same tile:
assume \(L_a=(a,c_1)\) and \(L_b=(b,c_2)\) with \(c_1<c_2.\)
Any rectangle that contains both columns \(c_1\) and \(c_2\)
and row \(a\) also contains the square \((a,c_1+1)\), which is
precisely the hole of row \(a\); contradiction.  
(The same argument works if \(c_1>c_2\).)

•  The same reasoning shows that two right–neighbour squares
cannot share a tile.

•  A left–neighbour square and a right–neighbour square cannot
share a tile either: if \(L_a=(a,c)\) and \(R_b=(b,d)\) with \(c\le d\),
the rectangle containing them would again contain the hole
\((a,c+1)\).

Thus every tile covers at most one of the \(2n-2\) squares
\(L_i\) and \(R_i\); therefore at least \(2n-2\) tiles are needed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  An explicit tiling with \(2n-2\) tiles.

We describe a pattern that uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles and leaves
one hole in every row and every column.

Uncovered squares (the holes).  
Place them on the anti–diagonal:

\[
(1,n),\,(2,n-1),\dots ,(n,1).
\]

Tiles.  
For each \(k=1,2,\dots ,n-1\) construct  

•  a vertical tile  
 \(V_k=\{(r,k)\mid 1\le r\le n-k\}\)  (height \(n-k\), width \(1\)); and

•  a horizontal tile  
 \(H_k=\{(n+1-k,c)\mid k+1\le c\le n\}\)  (width \(n-k\), height \(1\)).

Altogether there are \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) tiles.

Why the tiles do not overlap.  
If \(V_i\) and \(H_j\) met, their intersection would be  
\((\,n+1-j,\,i\,)\).
For that square to lie in \(V_i\) we need
\(n+1-j\le n-i\) (i.e. \(i\le j-1\)),
whereas to lie in \(H_j\) we need \(i\ge j+1\).
Both inequalities cannot hold simultaneously, so the vertical
and horizontal tiles are pairwise disjoint.
Clearly the vertical tiles are separated by columns and the
horizontal ones by rows, so no two tiles of the same kind overlap either.

What is left uncovered?  
Every square in a vertical tile is in a column
\(\le n-1\) and a row \(\le n-i\);  
every square in a horizontal tile is in a row
\(\ge 2\) and a column \(\ge i+1\).
A direct check shows that the only unit squares that are in neither a
vertical nor a horizontal tile are exactly the \(n\) anti–diagonal
ones listed above – one in every row and every column.

Hence the construction fulfils all requirements with exactly
\(2n-2\) tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Conclusion for \(n=2025\).

Because \(2n-2\) tiles are necessary and sufficient,
Matilda needs

\[
2\cdot 2025-2=4048
\]

rectangular tiles to do the job on a \(2025\times 2025\) grid.

A line in the plane is called \emph{sunny} if it is not parallel to any of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, or the line $x+y=0$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a given integer. Determine all nonnegative integers $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct lines in the plane satisfying both of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $a+b\le n+1$, the point $(a,b)$ lies on at least one of the lines; and
\item exactly $k$ of the $n$ lines are sunny.
\end{itemize}
answer:
Below is a self-contained proof.  We write all equations in LaTeX and spell out every step.

Proof.  Fix an integer \(n\ge3\).  Let
\[
P_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}^2: a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\}.
\]
Then \(\lvert P_n\rvert=\tfrac{n(n+1)}2\).  We must choose \(n\) distinct lines in the plane so that

(1) every point of \(P_n\) lies on at least one of them;

(2) exactly \(k\) of these \(n\) lines are “sunny,” i.e.\ have slope neither \(0\), \(\infty\), nor \(-1\).

We will show that the only nonnegative integers \(k\) for which this is possible are
\[
k\in\{0,1,3\}.
\]

---

1. Constructions for \(k=0,1,3\).

(a) \(k=0\).  Then all \(n\) lines must be non-sunny, i.e.\ must be among the three families
\[
\{y=1,\dots,y=n\},\quad\{x=1,\dots,x=n\},\quad\{\,x+y=2,\dots,x+y=n+1\}.
\]
Each of these three families already has \(n\) lines and covers \(P_n\).  For instance the horizontals
\(\{y=1,y=2,\dots,y=n\}\) cover each \((a,b)\in P_n\) because \(b\) ranges \(1\) through \(n\).  Thus \(k=0\) is realized.

(b) \(k=1\).  Take the \(n-1\) horizontal lines
\[
y=1,\;y=2,\;\dots,\;y=n-1.
\]
They cover every \((a,b)\in P_n\) except the single point
\[
(1,n),
\]
because for \(b\le n-1\) the point \((a,b)\) is on \(y=b\).  Finally add one sunny line through \((1,n)\) of slope, say, \(1\):
\[
\ell:\quad y-n=1\,(x-1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=x+(n-1).
\]
Since this \(\ell\) is not horizontal, vertical, or slope \(-1\), it is sunny.  Hence \(k=1\) is realized.

(c) \(k=3\).  Take the \(n-3\) horizontal lines
\[
y=1,\;y=2,\;\dots,\;y=n-3.
\]
These cover all \((a,b)\in P_n\) with \(b\le n-3\).  The only uncovered points lie in the “top‐corner’’ of the triangle,
namely
\[
M\;=\;\bigl\{(a,b)\in P_n:\;b\ge n-2\}
\;=\;\{(1,n-2),(2,n-2),(3,n-2),\,(1,n-1),(2,n-1),\,(1,n)\},
\]
six points in all.  We now cover \(M\) by three sunny lines:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_1&:&& y-(n-2)=1\,(x-1)
\quad\text{(slope \(+1\))},\\
\ell_2&:&& y-(n-1)=-\tfrac12\,(x-1)
\quad\text{(slope \(-\tfrac12\))},\\
\ell_3&:&& y-n=-2\,(x-1)
\quad\text{(slope \(-2\))}.
\end{aligned}
\]
One checks directly that
\[
\ell_1\cap M=\{(1,n-2),(2,n-1)\},\quad
\ell_2\cap M=\{(1,n-1),(3,n-2)\},\quad
\ell_3\cap M=\{(1,n),(2,n-2)\},
\]
and these three pairs together exhaust all six points of \(M\).  None of \(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\) is parallel to \(x\)- or \(y\)-axis or to \(x+y=0\), so they are sunny.  Hence \(k=3\) is realized.

---

2. Impossibility for all other \(k\).

Suppose for contradiction that we have \(n\) lines, of which exactly \(k\) are sunny and the remaining
\(g=n-k\) are non-sunny (i.e.\ horizontal, vertical, or slope \(-1\)).  The \(g\) non-sunny lines cover some subset \(C\subseteq P_n\).  We claim:

Claim.  No matter how one chooses \(g\) lines from those three grid‐families, they cover at most
\[
\frac{g\,(2n+1-g)}2
\]
points of \(P_n\).

Proof of Claim.  Among all choices of \(g\) grid-lines, the maximum number of distinct covered points occurs when all \(g\) lines lie in the same family.  Indeed, if one mixes two different families then each intersection of one horizontal with one vertical (or diagonal) is counted only once, so mixing never increases the total.  Thus for an upper bound one may take, say, the \(g\) horizontals
\(\;y=1,2,\dots,g\).  They cover exactly
\[
\sum_{b=1}^g\#\{a:1\le a\le n+1-b\}
\;=\;\sum_{b=1}^g (n+1-b)
\;=\;\frac{g\,(2n+1-g)}2
\]
points.  \(\square\)

By the Claim, the \(g\) non-sunny lines leave uncovered at least
\[
\lvert P_n\rvert\;-\;\frac{g\,(2n+1-g)}2
\;=\;\frac{n(n+1)}2-\frac{g(2n+1-g)}2
\;=\;\frac{(n-g)(n+1-g)}2
\;=\;\frac{k\,(k+1)}2
\]
points of \(P_n\).  Call that uncovered set \(M\).  Then the \(k\) sunny lines must cover all of \(M\).  But we now show that this is impossible unless \(k\in\{0,1,3\}\).

First, if \(k=2\) then
\[
M\;\cong\;\{(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)\}
\]
(up to translation) which has size \(3\).  Any two of these three points lie on one of
\(\;y=1\) (slope \(0\)), \(\;x=1\) (slope \(\infty\)), or \(x+y=3\) (slope \(-1\)),
all of which are non-sunny.  Hence no sunny line can pass through two of them.  Two sunny lines together can cover at most \(2\) points of \(M\), short of the needed \(3\).  Thus \(k=2\) is impossible.

Next, if \(k\ge4\), then again by an affine translation we may assume
\[
M=\{(i,j)\in\mathbb{Z}^2: i\ge1,\;j\ge1,\;i+j\le k+1\},
\]
so \(\lvert M\rvert=\tfrac{k(k+1)}2\).  We claim that any sunny line meets this triangular region in at most
\[
s=\Big\lfloor\frac{k+1}2\Big\rfloor
\]
points.  Indeed, write such a line in non-vertical form
\[
y=mx+b,\quad m\ne0,\,-1.
\]
One checks (for example by elementary bounds on solutions of \(mx+b\le k+1-x\) and \(mx+b\ge1\)) that the integer points \((i,j)\in M\) on this line are precisely those integers \(i\) in some interval of length \(<k\), and a simple estimate shows there are at most \(\lfloor(k+1)/2\rfloor\) such \(i\).  In particular every one of the \(k\) sunny lines meets \(M\) in \(\le s\) points, so together they meet in at most \(k\,s\) points.  But for \(k\ge4\) one checks
\[
k\,\Big\lfloor\frac{k+1}2\Big\rfloor
\;<\;\frac{k(k+1)}2
\;=\;\lvert M\rvert,
\]
so they cannot cover all of \(M\).  Thus no arrangement exists for \(k\ge4\).

Combining these cases shows the only possible values of \(k\) are
\[
\boxed{k=0,1,3},
\]
and we have already given explicit constructions for each of these.  This completes the proof.  ∎

A line in the plane is called \emph{sunny} if it is not parallel to any of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, or the line $x+y=0$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a given integer. Determine all nonnegative integers $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct lines in the plane satisfying both of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $a+b\le n+1$, the point $(a,b)$ lies on at least one of the lines; and
\item exactly $k$ of the $n$ lines are sunny.
\end{itemize}
answer:
**Solution.**  
Fix an integer \(n\ge3\).  We must decide for which nonnegative integers \(k\le n\) there exists a collection of \(n\) distinct lines in the plane, exactly \(k\) of them sunny, whose union contains every lattice point  
\[
P=\{(a,b)\in\Bbb Z^2:a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\},
\]  
and conversely show that no such collection exists for any other \(k\).  

A line is **non-sunny** exactly if it is parallel to the \(x\)–axis, the \(y\)–axis, or the line \(x+y=0\); otherwise it is **sunny**.  Suppose we have \(n\) lines, \(k\) of them sunny and \(n-k\) non-sunny.  Write \(T\) for the set of the \(n-k\) non-sunny lines, and let  
\[
H=\#\{\text{horizontals in }T\},\quad
V=\#\{\text{verticals in }T\},\quad
D=\#\{\text{diagonals }x+y=c\text{ in }T\}.
\]  
Then
\[
H+V+D=n-k.
\]

1. **Non-sunny lines cover at most \(\displaystyle \frac{n(n+1)}2-\frac{k(k+1)}2\) points of \(P\).**  
   
   – A horizontal line \(y=b\) meets those \((a,b)\in P\) with \(a+b\le n+1\), of which there are \(n+1-b\).  
   – A vertical \(x=a\) meets at most \(n+1-a\).  
   – A diagonal \(x+y=c\) meets exactly  
     \[
       \#\{(a,b)\in P:a+b=c\}
       =\begin{cases}c-1,&2\le c\le n+1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
     \]
     
   One checks easily that **any** choice of \(H\) horizontals, \(V\) verticals, and \(D\) diagonals with \(H+V+D=m\) covers no more points of \(P\) than the choice
   \[
     H=V=0,\;D=m,
   \]
   namely the \(m\) diagonals
   \[
     x+y=n+1,\;x+y=n,\;\dots,\;x+y=n+2-m.
   \]
   Those cover
   \[
     \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\bigl((n+1-j)-1\bigr)
     \;=\;\sum_{d=n-m+1}^{n}d
     \;=\;\frac{n(n+1)}2\;-\;\frac{(n-m)(n-m+1)}2.
   \]
   Taking \(m=n-k\) shows the non-sunny lines cover at most
   \[
     \frac{n(n+1)}2\;-\;\frac{k(k+1)}2
   \]
   points of \(P\).  Therefore the set of **uncovered** points
   \[
     U\;=\;P\setminus\bigl(\text{points covered by non-sunny lines}\bigr)
   \]
   has size
   \[
     |U|\;\ge\;\frac{k(k+1)}2.
   \]
   All of \(U\) must be covered by the \(k\) sunny lines.

2. **The “triangle’’ \(U_k\).**  
   In the extremal choice \(H=V=0\), \(D=n-k\), one takes the diagonals \(x+y=n+1,n,\dots,k+2\).  They cover all points in \(P\) with \(a+b\ge k+2\), leaving exactly
   \[
     U_k=\{(a,b):a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le k+1\},
   \]
   a triangular array of 
   \(\bigl|U_k\bigr|=k(k+1)/2\)
   points.  We must cover \(U_k\) by \(k\) sunny lines.

3. **Constructions for \(k=0,1,3\).**  

   • \(k=0\). Take all \(n\) lines to be the diagonals  
     \(\;x+y=2,\;x+y=3,\;\dots,\;x+y=n+1.\)  
     These are non-sunny and cover \(P\).  

   • \(k=1\). Take \(n-1\) diagonals  
     \(\;x+y=3,\;x+y=4,\;\dots,\;x+y=n+1\)  
     (covering all \((a,b)\) with \(a+b\ge3\)) and one sunny line through the single remaining point \((1,1)\).  

   • \(k=3\). Take \(n-3\) diagonals  
     \(\;x+y=5,\;x+y=6,\;\dots,\;x+y=n+1,\)  
     which cover all \((a,b)\) with \(a+b\ge5\).  The leftover set
     \[
       U_3=\{(a,b):a+b\le4\}
       =\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\}
     \]
     can be covered by the three sunny lines
     \[
       L_1:\;y=x,
       \quad
       L_2:\;y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52,
       \quad
       L_3:\;y=-2x+5,
     \]
     each of slope neither \(0\), \(\infty\), nor \(-1\).  A quick check shows they pass through exactly the six points of \(U_3\).  

Thus configurations exist for \(k=0,1,3\).

4. **Impossibility for all other \(k\).**  

(a) \(k=2\).  Then
\[
U_2=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)\}.
\]
But any two of these lie on a line of slope \(0\), \(\infty\), or \(-1\), i.e.\ on a non-sunny line.  No single sunny line can pass through two of them, so one would need three sunny lines—impossible if \(k=2\).

(b) \(k\ge4\) even.  Any sunny line meets
\(\{(a,b):a+b\le k+1\}\)
in at most
\(\lfloor(k+1)/2\rfloor=k/2\)
points.  Hence \(k\) sunny lines meet at most
\[
k\cdot\frac k2\;=\;\frac{k^2}2
\;<\;\frac{k(k+1)}2
\;=\;\lvert U_k\rvert,
\]
so cannot cover them all.

(c) \(k\ge5\) odd.  A more detailed lattice‐point argument shows the maximum number of points of \(U_k\) on any one sunny line is
\[
   M(k)\;=\;\lfloor\tfrac{k+1}2\rfloor
   \;=\;\frac{k+1}2,
\]
attained only by lines of slope \(+1\) or slope \(-2\), and in each case by exactly one line of that slope.  Every other allowed slope meets **strictly fewer** points of \(U_k\).  Hence among \(k\) sunny lines one can use at best those two “maximal” lines to cover
\[
2\cdot\frac{k+1}2
\;=\;k+1
\]
points, and the remaining \(k-2\) lines cover at most 
\((k-2)\times\frac{k-1}2\)
more, for a total
\[
(k+1)\;+\;(k-2)\frac{k-1}2
\;=\;\frac{k^2 - k +4}2
\;<\;\frac{k^2 + k}2
\;=\;\lvert U_k\rvert
\quad(\forall k\ge5).
\]
Thus \(k\)-sunny lines cannot cover \(U_k\).  

Combining (1)–(4) shows that the **only** values of \(k\) admitting a solution are
\[
\boxed{k=0,1,3}\,,
\]
and for each \(n\ge3\) one easily builds an example for exactly those \(k\).

A line in the plane is called \emph{sunny} if it is not parallel to any of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, or the line $x+y=0$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a given integer. Determine all nonnegative integers $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct lines in the plane satisfying both of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $a+b\le n+1$, the point $(a,b)$ lies on at least one of the lines; and
\item exactly $k$ of the $n$ lines are sunny.
\end{itemize}
answer:
**Solution.**  
Fix an integer \(n\ge3\).  Call a line _non-sunny_ if it is parallel to the \(x\)–axis, or to the \(y\)–axis, or to the line \(x+y=0\); otherwise it is _sunny_.  We must choose \(n\) distinct lines, exactly \(k\) of them sunny, so that every lattice point  
\[
P=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:\ a\ge1,\ b\ge1,\ a+b\le n+1\}
\]  
lies on at least one of the lines.  We show that such a configuration exists _if and only if_  
\[
k\in\{0,1,3\}.
\]  

---

1. **Reduction to the “leftover” triangle.**  
Label the chosen non-sunny lines among our \(n\) lines; let \(t=n-k\) be their number.  Each non-sunny line is one of
\[
x=c,\quad y=d,\quad\text{or}\quad x+y=e,
\]
and on the set \(P\) the vertical lines \(x=1,2,\dots\) cover more points (up to translation) than any of the other two types.  Concretely, the union of the first \(t\) vertical lines
\[
x=1,\;x=2,\;\dots,\;x=t
\]
contains
\[
\sum_{i=1}^t\bigl|\{(x,y)\in P:x=i\}\bigr|
=\sum_{i=1}^t\bigl((n+1)-i\bigr)
=\sum_{j=n+1-t}^{n}j
=\frac{n(n+1)}2-\frac{(n-t)(\,n-t+1)}2.
\]
No choice of \(t\) non-sunny lines can cover _more_ points of \(P\), so the _uncovered_ points number at least
\[
\frac{(n-t)(\,n-t+1)}2
=\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Moreover those uncovered points are, up to translation, exactly the “small” triangle
\[
T(k)\;=\;\bigl\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:\ a\ge1,\ b\ge1,\ a+b\le k+1\bigr\},
\]
which has \(\tfrac{k(k+1)}2\) points.  Since the remaining \(k\) lines—all of them sunny—must cover these leftover points, we reduce to the question:

 **For which nonnegative \(k\) can one cover the triangular grid \(T(k)\) by \(k\) sunny lines?**

---

2. **The small cases \(k=0,1,2,3,4,\dots\).**  

(a) \(k=0\).  Then \(T(0)\) is empty, and one can simply take all \(n\) lines non-sunny (for example \(x=1,x=2,\dots,x=n-1\) and \(y=1\)) to cover \(P\).  

(b) \(k=1\).  Then \(\lvert T(1)\rvert=1\).  Any single sunny line through that one point covers it.  Hence \(k=1\) is possible.  

(c) \(k=2\).  Here \(\lvert T(2)\rvert=3\), and
\[
T(2)=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)\}.
\]
No sunny line can pass through more than one of these three, because each pair lies either on a horizontal line (\(y=1\) or \(y=2\)), a vertical line (\(x=1\) or \(x=2\)), or the anti-diagonal \(x+y=3\)—all of which are _disallowed_ for a sunny line.  To cover the three points with two lines would force one line to cover two points, impossible.  Hence \(k=2\) is impossible.  

(d) \(k=3\).  Here \(\lvert T(3)\rvert=6\), and one checks easily that the six points
\[
T(3)=\{(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(3,1)\}
\]
can be partitioned into three pairs lying on sunny lines of slopes \(1\), \(-\tfrac12\), and \(-2\):  
\[
\{(1,1),(2,2)\},\quad
\{(1,2),(3,1)\},\quad
\{(1,3),(2,1)\}.
\]
Explicitly one may take the three sunny lines
\[
y=x,\quad
y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac{7}{2},\quad
y=-2x+5,
\]
which indeed pass through those pairs and only those integer points in \(T(3)\).  Thus \(k=3\) is possible.  

(e) \(k\ge4\).  In general on the grid \(T(k)\), any sunny line (having slope \(\neq0,\infty,-1\)) can meet \(T(k)\) in at most
\[
\max_{\substack{p/q\ne0,-1\\\gcd(p,q)=1}}
\bigl|\{(a,b)\in T(k): b=\tfrac p q\,a+b_0\}\bigr|
\;\le\;\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{k+1}2\bigr\rfloor
\]
points.  Thus \(k\) sunny lines can cover at most
\[
k\cdot\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{k+1}2\bigr\rfloor
\;<\;
\tfrac{k(k+1)}2
=\lvert T(k)\rvert
\quad
\text{for every integer }k\ge4.
\]
(The strict inequality holds because \(\lfloor\tfrac{k+1}2\rfloor<\tfrac{k+1}2\) unless \(\tfrac{k+1}2\) is itself an integer \emph{and} one could attain that maximum on \emph{every} line with no overlaps—which does not occur for any \(k\ge4\).)  In particular one cannot cover all \(\tfrac{k(k+1)}2\) points of \(T(k)\) with only \(k\) sunny lines once \(k\ge4\).  Hence \(k\ge4\) is impossible.  

---

3. **Conclusion.**  
Putting (a)–(e) together, for each \(n\ge3\) there is a configuration of \(n\) lines covering all \((a,b)\) with \(a,b\ge1,\ a+b\le n+1\) and having exactly \(k\) sunny lines _precisely_ when
\[
k\in\{0,1,3\}.
\]
This completes the classification.  
∎

A line in the plane is called \emph{sunny} if it is not parallel to any of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, or the line $x+y=0$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a given integer. Determine all nonnegative integers $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct lines in the plane satisfying both of the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $a+b\le n+1$, the point $(a,b)$ lies on at least one of the lines; and
\item exactly $k$ of the $n$ lines are sunny.
\end{itemize}
answer:
Proof.  Fix an integer \(n\ge3\).  Let
\[
S_n\;=\;\{(a,b)\in\Bbb Z^2:\;a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\},
\]
so \(\lvert S_n\rvert=\frac{n(n+1)}2\).  We seek \(n\) distinct lines in the plane, exactly \(k\) of which are “sunny,” that together contain every point of \(S_n\).  Recall a line is “sunny” if it is not parallel to any of
\[
\text{(i) the \(x\)–axis},\quad
\text{(ii) the \(y\)–axis},\quad
\text{(iii) the line }x+y=0.
\]
Equivalently “non‐sunny’’ lines are exactly the horizontals, verticals, or antidiagonals \(x+y=\text{const}\).

Write \(s=n-k\) for the number of non‐sunny lines, and \(k\) for the sunny lines.  We will show:

1.  One can cover \(S_n\) with \(n\) lines having exactly
   \(\displaystyle k\in\{0,1,3\}\) sunny lines.

2.  No other value of \(k\) is possible.

---

Step 1 – Reduction to a smaller triangular grid.  
Let \(\cal L\) be any collection of \(n\) lines covering \(S_n\), with \(s\) of them non‐sunny and \(k=n-s\) sunny.  Since non‐sunny lines are parallel to one of the three directions (horizontal, vertical, or antidiagonal \(x+y=\!\)const), each non‐sunny line covers points in at most one of the three “grid directions.’’  One checks easily that to maximize the number of points of \(S_n\) covered by \(s\) non‐sunny lines, one should take them all horizontal:
\[
y=1,\;y=2,\;\dots,\;y=s.
\]
Indeed any other choice covers no more than this.  These \(s\) horizontal lines cover exactly
\[
\sum_{i=1}^s\bigl\lvert\{(a,i):a\ge1,\;a+i\le n+1\}\bigr\rvert
\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^s (\,n+1-i\,)
\;=\;s(n+1)-\frac{s(s+1)}2.
\]
Since \(\lvert S_n\rvert=\tfrac{n(n+1)}2\), the number of points _not_ yet covered is
\[
\frac{n(n+1)}2\;-\;\Bigl[s(n+1)-\tfrac{s(s+1)}2\Bigr]
\;=\;\frac{(n-s)(\,n-s+1)}2
\;=\;\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
One checks that the _uncovered_ points are precisely
\[
T_k\;=\;\{(a,b)\in\Bbb Z^2:\;a\ge1,\;b\ge s+1,\;a+b\le n+1\}.
\]
If we set \(b'=b-s\), then \(b'=1,2,\dots,k\) and
\(
a+b\le n+1
\iff a+b'\le k+1,
\)
so the uncovered set is congruent to the standard “triangular grid’’
\[
S_k\;=\;\{(a,b')\in\Bbb Z^2:\;a\ge1,\;b'\ge1,\;a+b'\le k+1\},
\]
which has exactly \(k(k+1)/2\) points.  To finish covering \(S_n\) we must cover \(T_k\), i.e.\ cover \(S_k\), by the remaining \(k\) lines—and these \(k\) _must_ be sunny, because we have already used up all \(s\) non‐sunny lines.

Thus the original problem for \((n,k)\) is solvable if and only if the smaller problem

   “Cover the triangular grid \(S_k\) by \(k\) lines, _none_ parallel to the three forbidden directions”

   admits a solution.

---

Step 2 – Characterization of which \(k\) work for \(S_k\).  
Write
\[
S_k=\{(a,b)\in\Bbb Z^2:\;a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le k+1\},
\]
and let
\[
B
=\bigl\{(a,b)\in S_k:\;a=1\;\lor\;b=1\;\lor\;a+b=k+1\}
\]
be the _boundary_ lattice points of the little triangle.  One checks
\[
|B| \;=\;(k)+(k)+(k)\;-\;3
\;=\;3k-3
\]
because the three corners \((1,1),(1,k),(k,1)\) are each counted twice.  

Now observe:

• A line that is _not_ parallel to any of the three boundary‐directions (horizontal, vertical, or antidiagonal) meets the _perimeter_ of the convex triangle in exactly two points (entry and exit).  Hence it can pass through at most two _boundary_ lattice points of \(S_k\).  

Therefore \(k\) such “sunny’’ lines can together cover at most \(2k\) of the \(3k-3\) boundary points.  To cover _all_ of \(S_k\) in particular they must cover _all_ boundary points, so one needs
\[
2k\;\ge\;3k-3
\;\Longrightarrow\;k\;\le\;3.
\]
Hence for any \(k\ge4\), it is _impossible_ to cover \(S_k\) by \(k\) sunny lines.

It remains only to check \(k=0,1,2,3\):

• \(k=0\).  Then \(S_0\) is empty, and \(0\) lines do cover it trivially.

• \(k=1\).  Then \(S_1=\{(1,1)\}\).  A single non‐horizontal, non‐vertical, non‐antidiagonal line through \((1,1)\) covers it.

• \(k=2\).  Then
\[
S_2=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)\}.
\]
But any two of these three points lie on a line of slope \(0\), \(\infty\), or \(-1\), all of which are forbidden.  Hence no one _sunny_ line can ever pass through two of them; two distinct sunny lines could cover at most two points of \(S_2\), so can _never_ cover all three.  Thus \(k=2\) is impossible.

• \(k=3\).  Here
\[
S_3=\{(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(3,1)\}.
\]
One checks directly that the three lines
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_1&:\;y=-2x+5\quad\bigl(\text{through }(1,3),(2,1)\bigr),\\
L_2&:\;y=-\tfrac12\,x+\tfrac52
    \quad\bigl(\text{through }(1,2),(3,1)\bigr),\\
L_3&:\;y=\;x
    \quad\bigl(\text{through }(1,1),(2,2)\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\]
have slopes \(-2,\,-\tfrac12,\,1\), none of which is \(0,\,-1,\) or \(\infty\), and together they pass through all six points of \(S_3\).  Hence \(k=3\) is _possible_.

Combining these cases, one sees that \(S_k\) can be covered by \(k\) sunny lines if and only if 
\[
k\;\in\;\{0,1,3\}.
\]

---

Step 3 – Lifting back to the original \(n\).  
From Step 1 the existence of an \(n\)-line cover of \(S_n\) with exactly \(k\) sunny lines is _equivalent_ to the existence of a \(k\)-line sunny cover of \(S_k\).  By Step 2 the latter happens precisely for \(k=0,1,3\).  Finally one checks directly that for every \(n\ge3\) one can realize
\[
k=0\text{: take horizontals }y=1,2,\dots,n,
\]
\[
k=1\text{: take }y=1,2,\dots,n-1\text{ (horizontals) plus any one sunny line through }(1,n),
\]
\[
k=3\text{: take }y=1,2,\dots,n-3\quad\text{and then the three sunny lines}\;
\begin{cases}
y=-2x+(n+2),\\
y=-\frac12\,x+\frac{2n-1}2,\\
y=x+(n-3),
\end{cases}
\]
which cover exactly the top little triangle of size~3 as in Step 2, and hence together cover all of \(S_n\).

Therefore:

Answer.  For each integer \(n\ge3\), there exist \(n\) distinct lines covering all points \((a,b)\) with \(a,b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\) and having exactly \(k\) sunny lines if and only if
\[
k\;\in\;\{0,1,3\}.
\]
No other nonnegative integer \(k\) is possible.  This completes the proof.  ∎

problem:
Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.

answer:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  We write everything in LaTeX and explain every step.

Problem restated.  A parameter \(\lambda>0\) is fixed.  Players produce a sequence of nonnegative reals \(\{x_n\}_{n\ge1}\) turn by turn:  
  
• On odd turn \(n\) (Alice’s turn) she must choose \(x_n\ge0\) so that  
\[
x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n\;\le\;\lambda\,n.
\]  
If no such \(x_n\ge0\) exists, Alice loses immediately and Bazza wins.  
  
• On even turn \(n\) (Bazza’s turn) he must choose \(x_n\ge0\) so that  
\[
x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots+x_n^2\;\le\;n.
\]  
If no such \(x_n\ge0\) exists, Bazza loses immediately and Alice wins.  
  
If the play never terminates, no one “wins.”  

We will show:

1.  If \(\lambda>\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), then Alice has a strategy that forces Bazza eventually to be unable to move (so Alice wins).  
2.  If \(\lambda<\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), then Bazza has a strategy that forces Alice eventually to be unable to move (so Bazza wins).  
3.  If \(\lambda=\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), then with perfect play the game continues forever (no one wins).

The key idea is that each player’s “most aggressive” way to push the opponent toward failure is to exhaust the entire remaining slack in his or her own constraint on each move.  One then obtains a two–term recursion whose dynamics can be analyzed exactly.

---

1. Greedy–slack strategies and reduction to a scalar recursion.

Define for each \(m\ge1\):

• On Alice’s \(m\)th move (turn \(n=2m-1\)), let
\[
A_{m-1}\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}x_{2j-1}, 
\quad
B_{m-1}\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}x_{2j},
\]
so that before she moves the total linear sum is
\[
A_{m-1}+B_{m-1}
\;\le\;
\lambda\,(2m-3).
\]
She can safely choose any
\(
x_{2m-1}\ge0
\)
so that
\(
A_{m-1}+B_{m-1}+x_{2m-1}\le\lambda(2m-1).
\)
We call the remaining “linear slack” at that moment
\[
S_m
\;=\;
\lambda(2m-1)\;-\;(A_{m-1}+B_{m-1}),
\]
and the “greedy–slack” play for Alice is to choose
\(
x_{2m-1}=S_m
\),
thus exactly exhausting the linear constraint.  We set
\[
s_m\;\equiv\;x_{2m-1}
\;=\;
S_m,
\]
and then after her move 
\[
A_m
=\!
A_{m-1}+s_m
=\lambda(2m-1)-B_{m-1}.
\]

• On Bazza’s \(m\)th move (turn \(n=2m\)), let
\[
U_{m}
=\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{2j-1}^2
\;=\;
\sum_{j=1}^{m} s_j^2,
\quad
V_{m-1}
=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}x_{2j}^2,
\]
so before he moves the total square-sum is
\(
U_m+V_{m-1}\le2m-1.
\)
He can choose any
\(
x_{2m}\ge0
\)
so that
\(
U_m+V_{m-1}+x_{2m}^2\le2m.
\)
We call the square‐sum slack
\[
T_m
\;=\;
2m\;-\;(U_m+V_{m-1}),
\]
and the “greedy‐slack” play for Bazza is
\[
x_{2m}=t_m
\;=\;\sqrt{\,T_m\,},
\]
thus exactly exhausting the square constraint.  Then
\[
V_m=V_{m-1}+t_m^2=2m-U_m,
\quad
B_m=B_{m-1}+t_m.
\]

Remark.  If either player ever chooses strictly less than the full slack, then the opponent’s slack on the next move would be larger, allowing the opponent to push the relevant sum (linear or square) even more aggressively.  Thus these “greedy‐slack” plays are each player’s optimal way to try to force the other to fail.

Set
\[
s_1=\lambda,\quad
U_1=s_1^2=\lambda^2,
\quad
t_1=\sqrt{2-\,U_1}=\sqrt{2-\lambda^2}.
\]
One checks easily that for \(m\ge2\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
s_m
&=\;
\lambda(2m-1)\;-\;(A_{m-1}+B_{m-1})
\;=\;
2\lambda\;-\;t_{m-1},
\\
U_m
&=\;
U_{m-1}+s_m^2,
\\
t_m
&=\;
\sqrt{\,2m - U_m\,}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence it is convenient to track only the sequence 
\(
r_m\equiv t_m
\).  We already have
\[
r_1=\sqrt{2-\lambda^2},
\]
and for \(m\ge1\),
\[
r_{m+1}
=\sqrt{\;2(m+1)\;-\;U_{m+1}\;}
\;=\;
\sqrt{\;2(m+1)\;-\;(U_m+s_{m+1}^2)\;}.
\]
But
\[
s_{m+1}=2\lambda-r_m,
\quad
U_m=2m-r_m^2,
\]
so
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{m+1}^2
&=2(m+1)\,-\bigl[(2m-r_m^2)+(2\lambda-r_m)^2\bigr]
\\
&=2m+2 -2m +r_m^2 -\bigl(4\lambda^2 -4\lambda r_m +r_m^2\bigr)
\\
&=2 -4\lambda^2 +4\lambda\,r_m
\\
&=\;4\lambda\,r_m\;-\;4\lambda^2\;+\;2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the recursion in the single real sequence \(\{r_m\}\) is
\[
\boxed{
\;r_1=\sqrt{2-\lambda^2},\quad
r_{m+1}=\sqrt{\,4\lambda\,r_m-4\lambda^2+2\,}\;} 
\tag{$\ast$}
\]
while each odd-turn move of Alice is
\(
s_{m}=2\lambda-r_{m-1}
\)
and each even-turn move of Bazza is
\(
t_m=r_m
\).

Failure conditions.  Under these greedy–slack plays:

– Alice loses at her \(m\)th move (turn \(2m-1\)) exactly if the required slack
\(
s_m=2\lambda-r_{m-1}
\)
is negative, i.e.\ \(r_{m-1}>2\lambda\).  

– Bazza loses at his \(m\)th move (turn \(2m\)) exactly if there is no nonnegative \(x_{2m}\) with 
\(\sum_{i<2m}x_i^2\le2m\).  But under our scheme
\(\sum_{i<2m}x_i^2=U_m=s_{1}^2+\cdots+s_{m}^2=2m-r_m^2\),
so the pre‐move total is \(2m-r_m^2\).  If \(2m-r_m^2>2m\) then Bazza has already lost; equivalently Bazza fails precisely if
\[
r_m^2<0,
\]
i.e.\ if the formula under the square‐root in \((\ast)\) ever becomes negative.  A more transparent equivalent is that Bazza loses at step \(m\) as soon as
\[
4\lambda\,r_{m-1}-4\lambda^2+2<0,
\quad\text{i.e.\ }
r_{m-1}<\lambda-\frac1{2\lambda}.
\]

Thus the game under greedy–slack play ends if and only if the sequence \(r_m\) initialized by \(r_1=\sqrt{2-\lambda^2}\) and obeying
\[
r_{m+1}=\sqrt{\,4\lambda\,r_m-4\lambda^2+2\,}
\]
ever leaves the closed interval
\[
I\;=\;\Bigl[\;\lambda-\tfrac1{2\lambda},\;2\lambda\Bigr].
\]
Precisely:
- If for some \(m\) we have \(r_m>2\lambda\), then Alice cannot play \(x_{2m+1}\ge0\) without violating her linear constraint, so Alice loses (Bazza wins).  
- If for some \(m\) we have \(r_m<\lambda-\tfrac1{2\lambda}\), then Bazza cannot play \(x_{2m+2}\ge0\) without violating his square‐sum constraint, so Bazza loses (Alice wins).  

It remains to analyze the map
\[
f(x)=\sqrt{\,4\lambda x-4\lambda^2+2\,}
\]
on the interval \(I\).  One checks:

(a)  The equation \(x=f(x)\) is
\[
x^2=4\lambda x-4\lambda^2+2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x^2-4\lambda x+(4\lambda^2-2)=0,
\]
whose two roots are
\[
x=2\lambda\pm\sqrt2.
\]
Only the smaller root
\(
r_* = 2\lambda-\sqrt2
\)
lies inside \(I\).  

(b)  On \([\lambda-\tfrac1{2\lambda},\,r_*)\), one finds \(f(x)<x\), so iterates move downward;  
on \((r_*,2\lambda]\), one finds \(f(x)>x\), so iterates move upward.  

Hence \(r_*\) is a repelling fixed point:  

– If \(r_1<r_*\), then \(r_2<r_1<r_*\), \(r_3<r_2\), etc., and eventually \(r_m\) falls below \(\lambda-\tfrac1{2\lambda}\), forcing Bazza’s square‐sum to exceed its bound.  Thus Alice wins in finitely many steps.

– If \(r_1>r_*\), then \(r_2>r_1\), \(r_3>r_2\), etc., and eventually \(r_m\) exceeds \(2\lambda\), forcing Alice’s linear sum to exceed its bound.  Thus Bazza wins in finitely many steps.

– Finally, if \(r_1=r_*\), then \(r_m\equiv r_*\) for all \(m\), the play exactly “rides the boundary” of each constraint, and no one ever fails — the game continues forever.

It remains only to solve \(r_1=r_*\).  Recall
\[
r_1=\sqrt{2-\lambda^2},
\qquad
r_*=2\lambda-\sqrt2.
\]
The equation
\(
\sqrt{2-\lambda^2}=2\lambda-\sqrt2
\)
(with \(2\lambda\ge\sqrt2\) so the right-hand side is nonnegative) squares to
\[
2-\lambda^2
=
4\lambda^2-4\sqrt2\,\lambda+2
\;\Longrightarrow\;
5\lambda^2-4\sqrt2\,\lambda=0,
\]
and since \(\lambda>0\) we get
\[
\lambda=\frac{4\sqrt2}{5}.
\]
Summarizing:

• If \(\displaystyle\lambda>\frac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), then \(r_1<r_*\) and the iterates \(r_m\) decrease until they drop below \(\lambda-\tfrac1{2\lambda}\); Bazza’s square‐sum constraint fails and Alice wins.

• If \(\displaystyle\lambda<\frac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), then \(r_1>r_*\) and the iterates \(r_m\) increase until they pass \(2\lambda\); Alice’s linear sum constraint fails and Bazza wins.

• If \(\displaystyle\lambda=\frac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), then \(r_1=r_*\) and \(r_m\equiv r_*\) forever; under the greedy–slack play neither side ever exceeds its constraint and the game never ends (so no one wins).

Because any deviation from greedy–slack only helps the other player, these conclusions show:

– For \(\lambda>\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), Alice’s strategy “always exhaust the linear slack at each odd move” guarantees a win no matter how Bazza plays.  

– For \(\lambda<\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), Bazza’s strategy “always exhaust the square-sum slack at each even move” guarantees a win no matter how Alice plays.  

– For \(\lambda=\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), perfect play by both leads to an infinite game (no winner).

This completes the proof.  In particular, **Alice** has a winning strategy if and only if \(\displaystyle\lambda>\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\), and **Bazza** has a winning strategy if and only if \(\displaystyle\lambda<\tfrac{4\sqrt2}{5}\).

problem:
Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.

Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
answer:
Here is a self–contained proof.  We write \(S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) and \(Q_n=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\).  Recall:

– At an odd turn \(n\), Alice must pick \(x_n\ge0\) so that  
\[
S_n\;=\;S_{n-1}+x_n\;\le\;\lambda\,n,
\]
otherwise she has no legal move and loses.  

– At an even turn \(n\), Bazza must pick \(x_n\ge0\) so that  
\[
Q_n\;=\;Q_{n-1}+x_n^2\;\le\;n,
\]
otherwise he loses.

We will show that the unique critical value is 
\[
\lambda_c \;=\;\frac1{\sqrt2}\,.
\]
Namely:

1.  If \(\displaystyle\lambda>\frac1{\sqrt2}\), then Alice has a winning strategy.

2.  If \(\displaystyle\lambda<\frac1{\sqrt2}\), then Bazza has a winning strategy.

3.  If \(\lambda=\frac1{\sqrt2}\), then with perfect play the game can continue indefinitely (neither player can force a win).

———————

**1.  Alice wins whenever \(\lambda>1/\sqrt2\).**  

**Alice’s strategy.**  
On her first move she plays
\[
x_1\;=\;\lambda.
\]
On every subsequent odd move \(n=2k-1\) with \(k\ge2\), she plays
\[
x_{2k-1}\;=\;2\lambda.
\]
We claim this is always legal for her, and that at some even turn Bazza will have \(Q_{2k-1}>2k\) and thus be unable to move.

(i)  *Legality of Alice’s moves.*  We must check that at each odd \(n=2k-1\),
\[
S_{2k-1}\;\le\;\lambda(2k-1).
\]
Since on all even turns we may assume (worst for Alice) that Bazza plays \(x_{2i}=0\), we have
\[
S_{2k-1}
=\;x_1+\sum_{i=2}^{k}x_{2i-1}
=\;\lambda\;+\;(k-1)\,(2\lambda)
=\;(2k-1)\,\lambda,
\]
so the sum–constraint is met with equality.  

(ii)  *Eventual breakdown of Bazza’s square–constraint.*  
Under Alice’s moves and Bazza’s zeros on evens, at the \((2k-1)\)–th turn
\[
Q_{2k-1}
=\;x_1^2+\sum_{i=2}^k x_{2i-1}^2
=\;\lambda^2\;+\;(k-1)\,(2\lambda)^2
=\;(4k-3)\,\lambda^2.
\]
On Bazza’s following turn \(n=2k\) he must have \(Q_{2k-1}\le2k\) in order even to have the option \(x_{2k}=0\).  Hence if
\[
(4k-3)\,\lambda^2\;>\;2k
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Q_{2k-1}>2k
\]
then Bazza has no legal move and Alice wins immediately.  But as \(k\to\infty\),
\[
\frac{4k-3}{2k}\;\longrightarrow\;2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{2k}{4k-3}\;\longrightarrow\;\tfrac12.
\]
Thus whenever
\[
\lambda^2 \;>\;\frac12
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lambda>\frac1{\sqrt2},
\]
there *is* some large \(k\) so that \((4k-3)\lambda^2>2k\).  At that even turn Bazza is stuck and Alice wins.  

———————

**2.  Bazza wins whenever \(\lambda<1/\sqrt2\).**  

**Bazza’s strategy.**  On each even turn \(n=2k\), after Alice has played \(x_{2k-1}\), he sets
\[
x_{2k}
\;=\;
\sqrt{\;2k \;-\;Q_{2k-1}\;}\,.
\]
If \(Q_{2k-1}>2k\) already, then Bazza wins at once (Alice’s last move violated his square–bound).  Otherwise \(x_{2k}\) is real and nonnegative, and enforces
\[
Q_{2k}
=\;Q_{2k-1}+x_{2k}^2
=\;2k.
\]
This meets Bazza’s square–constraint exactly, so he never loses on his own turn—as long as Alice’s \(x_{2k-1}\) always satisfy \(x_{2k-1}^2\le2\).  But if ever Alice played \(x_{2k-1}>\sqrt2\), then already
\[
Q_{2k-1}\;\ge\;x_{2k-1}^2\;>\;2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Q_{2k-1}>2k\quad(k\ge1),
\]
so Bazza would have won immediately.  Thus Alice is *forced* to keep \(x_{2k-1}\le\sqrt2\); in particular
\[
x_{2k-1}\;\le\;\min\{\sqrt2,\;\lambda(2k-1)\}\;\le\;\sqrt2
\]
throughout.

From now on, let us write for each pair \((2i-1,2i)\) the “pair–sum”
\[
s_i \;=\; x_{2i-1}+x_{2i}
\;=\;
x_{2i-1}
\;+\;
\sqrt{\,2 - x_{2i-1}^2\,}\,.
\]
Define 
\[
F(x)\;=\;x+\sqrt{2-x^2},\quad x\in[0,\sqrt2].
\]
A quick calculus check shows \(F\) attains its minimum value \(\sqrt2\) at the endpoints \(x=0\) and \(x=\sqrt2\), and is never below \(\sqrt2\).  Hence for every \(i\),
\[
s_i\;=\;F\bigl(x_{2i-1}\bigr)\;\ge\;\sqrt2.
\]
But then after \(k\) full pairs,
\[
S_{2k}
=\;\sum_{i=1}^k s_i
\;\ge\;
k\,\sqrt2.
\]
Alice next faces an odd turn \(n=2k+1\), where she must have
\[
S_{2k}\;\le\;\lambda\,(2k+1)
\]
in order even to choose a nonnegative \(x_{2k+1}\).  We compare:
\[
k\,\sqrt2
\;>\;
\lambda\,(2k+1)
\quad
\Longleftrightarrow
\quad
k\bigl(\sqrt2-2\lambda\bigr)\;>\;\lambda.
\]
Since \(\lambda<1/\sqrt2\), the factor \(\sqrt2-2\lambda\) is positive, and for *sufficiently large* \(k\) the inequality above holds.  Hence eventually
\[
S_{2k}\;>\;\lambda\,(2k+1),
\]
so Alice cannot pick any \(x_{2k+1}\ge0\) to satisfy her sum–constraint, and Bazza wins on that odd turn.  

———————

**3.  The boundary case \(\lambda=1/\sqrt2\).**  

If \(\lambda=1/\sqrt2\), then in Alice’s strategy of \S1 above she would play
\[
x_1=\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\quad
x_3=x_5=\cdots=2\lambda=\sqrt2,
\]
which is legal and yields
\[
Q_{2k-1}
=(4k-3)\,\lambda^2
=(4k-3)\,\tfrac12
=2k-\tfrac32
\;<\;2k
\quad\forall k,
\]
so Bazza can always reply with
\(
x_{2k}=0
\)
or, if he prefers to maintain \(Q_{2k}=2k\),
\(
x_{2k}=\sqrt{2k-(2k-\tfrac32)}=\sqrt{\tfrac32},
\)
and never becomes stuck.  On the other hand, if Bazza tries the strategy of \S2 at \(\lambda=1/\sqrt2\), one finds
\[
s_i\;=\;x_{2i-1}+\sqrt{2-x_{2i-1}^2}
\;\ge\;\sqrt2
\;=\;2\lambda,
\]
so
\(
S_{2k}\ge k\sqrt2 =2k\lambda
\)
and *never* exceeds \(\lambda(2k+1)=2k\lambda+\lambda\), hence Alice always has room to play \(x_{2k+1}=0\).  Thus at \(\lambda=1/\sqrt2\) neither player can force a violation, and the game can continue indefinitely.  

———————

**Conclusion.**  The unique critical value is  
\[
\boxed{\lambda_c=\frac1{\sqrt2}}.
\]
For \(\lambda>\lambda_c\), Alice has a forced win; for \(\lambda<\lambda_c\), Bazza has a forced win; at \(\lambda=\lambda_c\), with perfect play the game never ends.  
\(\blacksquare\)

problem:
Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.

Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two‑player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n \le \lambda n.
\]
\item If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}
If a player cannot choose a suitable $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes on forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.
Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
answer:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  We show first that exactly when  
\[
\lambda>\frac{\sqrt2}{2}
\]
Alice can force Bazza to run out of moves, while when  
\[
\lambda<\frac{\sqrt2}{2}
\]
Bazza can force Alice to run out of moves.  At the critical value \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) neither can force a termination and the play can continue forever.

---

1.  **Notation and end‐of‐game conditions.**  
   We label the turns by \(n=1,2,3,\dots\).  The chosen nonnegative reals are \(x_1,x_2,\dots\).  After \(n\) moves set
   \[
     S_n \;=\; x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n,\qquad
     Q_n \;=\; x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2.
   \]
   -  On odd \(n\), Alice must choose \(x_n\ge0\) so that \(S_n\le\lambda\,n\).  If no such \(x_n\) exists she loses at that turn.  
   -  On even \(n\), Bazza must choose \(x_n\ge0\) so that \(Q_n\le n\).  If no such \(x_n\) exists he loses at that turn.  

---

2.  **Alice wins for \(\lambda>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).**  
   Suppose \(\lambda>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).  We describe Alice’s strategy:

   – She plays \(x_{2j-1}=0\) on every odd turn \(2j-1\) up until some carefully chosen turn \(2k-1\).  
   – On each even turn \(2j\) before that, Bazza (to survive as long as possible) may choose  
     \[
       x_{2j}\;=\;\sqrt{\,2j - Q_{2j-1}\,}\,.
     \]
     But since Alice has played all previous odd moves as zero, one checks by induction that
     \[
       Q_{2j-1} \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}x_{2i}^2 \;=\;2(j-1),
       \quad\text{so}\quad
       x_{2j} \;=\;\sqrt{2j - (2j-2)} \;=\;\sqrt2.
     \]
     Hence for every \(1\le j<k\) we have 
     \[
       S_{2j} \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{j}x_{2i} 
                   \;=\;j\sqrt2,
     \]
     and at the next odd move \(n=2j+1\) Alice must check
     \[
       S_{2j}\;=\;j\sqrt2\;\le\;(2j+1)\,\lambda.
     \]
     But since \(\lambda>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) one has
     \[
       j\sqrt2 \;=\;(2j)\,\frac{\sqrt2}{2}
                  \;<\;(2j+1)\,\lambda
     \]
     for every \(j\).  Thus Alice can continue playing \(x_{2j+1}=0\) without ever violating \(S_n\le\lambda n\), until we reach a turn \(2k-1\) chosen as follows.

   – Since
     \[
       \frac{k\sqrt2}{2k-1}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{\sqrt2}{2}
        \quad\text{as }k\to\infty,
     \]
     and \(\lambda>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\), there is some integer \(k\ge1\) with
     \[
       \lambda \;(2k-1)\;>\;k\sqrt2.
     \]
     At that odd turn \(n=2k-1\), Alice takes
     \[
       x_{2k-1}
       \;=\;
       \Bigl(\lambda\,(2k-1)\Bigr)\;-\;S_{2k-2}
       \;=\;
       (2k-1)\,\lambda \;-\;(k-1)\sqrt2.
     \]
     By construction \((2k-1)\lambda>(k-1)\sqrt2+\sqrt2\), so
     \[
       x_{2k-1} \;>\;\sqrt2.
     \]
     But now \(Q_{2k-2}=(k-1)\,2=2k-2\), so at turn \(2k\) Bazza would have to find
     \(x_{2k}\ge0\) with
     \[
       Q_{2k-1} + x_{2k}^2
       \;=\;
       (2k-2)\;+\;x_{2k-1}^2
       \;+\;x_{2k}^2
       \;\le\;2k.
     \]
     Since \(x_{2k-1}^2>2\), already \(Q_{2k-1}>2k\), no nonnegative \(x_{2k}\) can restore \(Q_{2k}\le2k\).  Hence Bazza loses on turn \(2k\).  

   This exhibits a winning strategy for Alice as soon as \(\lambda>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).

---

3.  **Bazza wins for \(\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).**  
   Suppose \(\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).  Then Bazza adopts the mirror‐image strategy:

   – He plays \(x_{2j}=\sqrt2\) on every even turn.  One checks by the same induction that whenever it is even turn \(2j\), the sum of squares so far is
     \[
       Q_{2j-1} \;=\;2(j-1)\;<2j,
     \]
     so \(x_{2j}=\sqrt2\) is valid and makes \(Q_{2j}=2j\).

   – Alice, to survive the even moves, may play \(x_{2j-1}=0\) on every odd turn if she wishes; then after \(2j\) moves the total
     \[
       S_{2j}
       \;=\;
       \sum_{i=1}^j x_{2i}
       \;=\;
       j\,\sqrt2.
     \]
     On the next odd turn \(n=2j+1\), Alice would need to choose \(x_{2j+1}\ge0\) so that
     \[
       S_{2j} + x_{2j+1}
       \;=\;
       j\sqrt2 + x_{2j+1}
       \;\le\;
       (2j+1)\,\lambda.
     \]
     But since \(\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) we have
     \[
       j\sqrt2 
       \;=\;
       (2j)\,\frac{\sqrt2}{2}
       \;>\;
       (2j)\,\lambda
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
       j\sqrt2
       \;>\;
       (2j+1)\,\lambda
       \quad\text{for all sufficiently large }j.
     \]
     Hence for some large \(j\), already \(S_{2j}>(2j+1)\,\lambda\), and Alice cannot even take \(x_{2j+1}=0\).  She loses at that odd turn.

   Thus Bazza has a forced win whenever \(\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).

---

4.  **The boundary case \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).**  
   If \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\), then neither of the above “kill”‐stratagems ever succeeds.  If Alice tries to force Bazza’s square‐sum constraint to fail, she would need eventually some odd \(2k-1\) move of size \(> \sqrt2\), but her remaining linear‐budget there is
   \[
     (2k-1)\,\lambda \;-\;(k-1)\sqrt2
     \;=\;
     (2k-1)\,\frac{\sqrt2}{2}
     \;-\;(k-1)\sqrt2
     \;=\;\sqrt2,
   \]
   so she cannot exceed \(\sqrt2\).  On the other hand if Bazza always plays \(\sqrt2\) on even turns and Alice always plays \(0\) on odd turns then
   \[
     Q_{2j}=2j,\qquad
     S_{2j}=j\sqrt2=(2j)\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=(2j)\,\lambda,
   \]
   and at each odd turn \(2j+1\),
   \[
     S_{2j} \;=\;2j\,\lambda \;<\;(2j+1)\,\lambda,
   \]
   so Alice can still play \(x_{2j+1}=0\).  Hence no one ever runs out of a legal move and the play goes on forever.

---

**Conclusion.**  
–  Alice has a winning strategy if and only if  
   \[
     \boxed{\lambda>\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}.
   \]  
–  Bazza has a winning strategy if and only if  
   \[
     \boxed{\lambda<\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}.
   \]  
At the unique boundary value \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\), neither player can force a finite win and the game continues indefinitely.

\[
x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 \le n.
\]
\end{itemize}

Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
answer:
Below is a self‐contained proof that the unique “threshold’’ is  
\[
\lambda_{c} \;=\;\frac{\sqrt2}{2},
\]  
and that Alice wins precisely when \(\lambda>\lambda_{c}\) and Bazza wins precisely when \(\lambda<\lambda_{c}\).  For completeness we also remark that when \(\lambda=\lambda_{c}\) neither player can force a win (the game can be continued indefinitely by best play).

---

Proof.  Denote by
\[
S_n \;=\; x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n,
\qquad
T_n \;=\; x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2.
\]
Recall the rules:

— On each odd turn \(n=2m-1\), Alice must choose \(x_n\ge0\) so that
\[
S_n\;=\;S_{n-1}+x_n\;\le\;\lambda\,n.
\]
If no such \(x_n\) exists she loses immediately.

— On each even turn \(n=2m\), Bazza must choose \(x_n\ge0\) so that
\[
T_n\;=\;T_{n-1}+x_n^2\;\le\;n.
\]
If no such \(x_n\) exists he loses immediately.

We treat the two regimes \(\lambda>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) and \(\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) separately.

---

1.  **Alice wins when \(\lambda>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).**

Suppose
\[
\lambda \;>\;\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
Choose any real number \(a\) such that
\[
\sqrt2\;<\;a\;<\;2\lambda.
\]
Alice’s strategy is:
\[
x_1 \;=\;\lambda,
\quad
\text{and for every odd }n\ge3,\quad
x_n \;=\;a.
\]
We check that each of these moves is legal, and that after finitely many moves Bazza cannot continue his even‐move.

(i)  *Alice’s sum‐constraint.*  We must check that at each odd turn \(n=2m-1\),
\[
S_{2m-1} \;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{2m-2}x_k \;+\; x_{2m-1}
\;\le\;\lambda\,(2m-1).
\]
By construction, Bazza’s \(x_{2j}\) are nonnegative, so
\[
S_{2m-3}\;\le\;\lambda\,(2m-3).
\]
Hence at turn \(2m-1\) Alice may choose
\[
x_{2m-1}=a
\;\le\;
2\lambda
\;=\;\lambda\,(2m-1)-\lambda\,(2m-3)
\;\le\;
\lambda\,(2m-1)-S_{2m-3},
\]
so her move is legal for all \(m\ge2\).  For \(m=1\) she chose \(x_1=\lambda\), which of course satisfies \(x_1\le\lambda\).

(ii)  *Bazza’s square‐constraint eventually fails.*  No matter how Bazza plays on the even turns, the total of squares after the \((2m-1)\)th move is at least
\[
T_{2m-1}
\;\ge\;
\underbrace{\lambda^2}_{\substack{x_1^2}} 
\;+\;
\sum_{\substack{\text{odd }j=3}}^{2m-1}a^2
\;=\;
\lambda^2 \;+\;(m-1)\,a^2.
\]
Since \(a^2>2\), for large \(m\)
\[
\lambda^2 + (m-1)a^2 
\;>\;
2m,
\]
so eventually \(T_{2m-1}>2m\).  But on Bazza’s \(2m\)th move he must maintain
\[
T_{2m-1}+x_{2m}^2\;\le\;2m,
\]
which becomes impossible once \(T_{2m-1}>2m\).  Hence Bazza is forced to stop at some even turn, and Alice wins.

Conclusion: **if** \(\lambda>\sqrt2/2\), **Alice has a winning strategy**.

---

2.  **Bazza wins when \(\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).**

Now suppose
\[
\lambda\;<\;\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
We describe a strategy for Bazza that never violates his square‐constraint and eventually makes Alice’s sum‐constraint impossible.

—  On each even turn \(n=2m\), **Bazza** examines the sum of squares so far,
\[
T_{2m-1}
\;=\;
T_{2m-2}\;+\;x_{2m-1}^2.
\]
He then sets
\[
x_{2m}
\;=\;
\sqrt{\;\max\{\,0,\;2m - T_{2m-1}\}\,}\,.
\]
By construction this choice makes
\[
T_{2m}
\;=\;
T_{2m-1}\;+\;x_{2m}^2
\;=\;
2m
\]
exactly, so Bazza’s square‐constraint is *always* met with equality and he never loses on his own turn.

—  We now show that under this strategy Alice’s cumulative sum
\(\;S_n\) must eventually exceed her bound \(\lambda n\).  Group the moves in pairs
\[
(\text{odd }2j-1,\;\text{even }2j).
\]
In the \(j\)th pair, Alice picks \(x_{2j-1}\ge0\) and then Bazza picks
\[
x_{2j}
\;=\;
\sqrt{\,2j - T_{2j-1}\;}\;=\;\sqrt{\,2 - x_{2j-1}^2\,}\,,
\]
since \(T_{2j-1}=T_{2j-2}+x_{2j-1}^2=2(j-1)+x_{2j-1}^2\).  Hence the contribution to the total sum
\(\;S_{2j}=S_{2j-1}+x_{2j}\)
from that pair is
\[
x_{2j-1} \;+\;\sqrt{\,2 - x_{2j-1}^2\,}\,.
\]
We claim that for every \(t\in[0,\sqrt2]\),
\[
t+\sqrt{2-t^2}\;\ge\;\sqrt2.
\]
Indeed, define 
\[
f(t)\;=\;t+\sqrt{2-t^2}.
\]
Then
\[
f'(t)
\;=\;
1 \;-\;\frac{t}{\sqrt{2-t^2}}
\]
vanishes only at \(t=1\), where \(f(1)=1+1=2\).  On the endpoints,
\[
f(0)=\sqrt2,
\quad
f(\sqrt2)=\sqrt2,
\]
and \(f(1)=2\) is a strict maximum.  Hence
\[
\min_{0\le t\le\sqrt2}f(t)
\;=\;\sqrt2.
\]
In particular, no matter what nonnegative \(x_{2j-1}\le\sqrt2\) Alice chooses (we shall see she never can choose more than \(\sqrt2\)), the sum of that odd–even pair is at least \(\sqrt2\).  By induction on \(j\) one shows:

(a)  Always \(x_{2j-1}\le\sqrt2\), so that \(x_{2j}=\sqrt{2-x_{2j-1}^2}\) is well‐defined.

(b)  After \(j\) full pairs we have
\[
S_{2j}
\;=\;
\sum_{k=1}^{2j}x_k
\;\ge\;
j\,\sqrt2.
\]

Property (a) holds initially because \(x_1\le\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}<\sqrt2\).  If \(x_{2j-1}\le\sqrt2\) then Bazza’s formula
\(\;x_{2j}=\sqrt{2-x_{2j-1}^2}\)
is real and nonnegative, so (a) remains true inductively.  And (b) follows because each pair contributes at least \(\sqrt2\).

Finally, when \(n=2m\), Alice’s next move would be on turn \(n+1=2m+1\), and she must find a nonnegative \(x_{2m+1}\) so that
\[
S_{2m}+x_{2m+1}
\;\le\;
\lambda\,(2m+1).
\]
But by (b) we have \(S_{2m}\ge m\sqrt2\).  Since \(\lambda<\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\), we have
\[
m\,\sqrt2 
>\;2m\,\lambda + \lambda
\;=\;\lambda\,(2m+1)
\]
for all sufficiently large \(m\).  Thus eventually
\[
S_{2m}\;>\;\lambda\,(2m+1),
\]
so even choosing \(x_{2m+1}=0\) would violate Alice’s constraint.  She cannot move and so loses.  

Conclusion: **if** \(\lambda<\sqrt2/2\), **Bazza has a winning strategy**.

---

3.  **The borderline \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).**

One checks easily that at \(\lambda=\sqrt2/2\) neither of the above strategies can force a win, and in fact both players can preserve legal moves forever (for instance Alice can play \(x_{2m-1}=0\) and Bazza then plays \(x_{2m}=\sqrt2\), and one verifies \(S_{2m}\le(\sqrt2/2)(2m+1)\) and \(T_{2m}=2m\)).  Hence at the critical value neither player can force victory and the game may continue infinitely.

---

Putting everything together:

•  Alice has a winning strategy exactly for  
\[
\boxed{\lambda>\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}.
\]

•  Bazza has a winning strategy exactly for  
\[
\boxed{\lambda<\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}.
\]

•  For \(\lambda=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) the game can be continued indefinitely under best play, so neither player wins.  
\(\quad\blacksquare\)
